entries.title: Lincoln Park Zoo mourns 'larger than life' snow leopard Ozzy
entries.summary: <p>Lincoln Park Zoo announced the passing of its longtime snow leopard Ozzy “following a rapid deterioration in his health.”</p><p>Zoo officials said visitors knew 8-year-old Ozzy by his bushy tail, which would hang down as he took afternoon naps, and his bursts of energy. The snow leopard would often be seen running around the habitat with his mate, Kennedi, and climbing up the rocky wall at the back of the enclosure.</p><p>Those who worked with the animal said he enjoyed training sessions. His favorite treat was chicken puree.</p><p>“Ozzy touched the lives of so many — both guests and staff alike — and quickly became a favorite of every keeper who had the honor of working with him,” said the zoo’s Curator of Mammals Cassy Kutilek. “He had a stoic yet playful personality that was a perfect balance to his mate Kennedi’s exuberance.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> the Pepper Family Wildlife Center opened, according to the zoo.</p><p>The International Union for Conservation of Nature considers snow leopards endangered, citing ongoing threats from poaching and climate change that impact their natural habitats in Central Asia’s mountainous regions.</p><p>While snow leopards are considered solitary animals, per the zoo’s animal experts, Ozzy and his mate often spent time together. Zoo officials said they will also monitor Kennedi's behavior in the coming weeks.</p><p>“Ozzy’s loss is felt throughout the entire Lincoln Park Zoo family,” the zoo said in a statement. “His larger-than-life personality will be missed by zoo staff, volunteers, and visitors alike.”</p>

entries.title: Experienced, stronger Juel Pryor sparks Lindblom past South Shore
entries.summary: <p>Lindblom quarterback Juel Pryor “throws a beautiful ball,” according to his coach, Tyrice Jackson.</p><p>“This is his third season as the starter, and he is probably the best thrower in the city,” Jackson said.</p><p>Pryor’s strong arm and experienced decision-making were on display in the Eagles’ 28-6 victory against South Shore on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/08/27/high-school-football-scores-chicago-illinois" >Thursday</a> at Eckersall Stadium.</p><p>Pryor says his offseason training program, adding weight and muscle, is the key to actually displaying that beautiful ball.</p><p>“I needed to grow my body to be able to take hits,” Pryor said. “[My trainer] helped me build my body over the offseason.”</p><p>Lindblom (2-0) won just two games last season and three in Pryor’s first year on varsity. The Eagles returned 11 starters this season and 40 players overall.</p><p>“The last couple of years we have been young,” Jackson said. “We’ve had leads and lost them late. Now we have skill, and we are mature seniors and juniors. We should be able to run the ball and throw the ball on just about anybody and put teams away.”</p><p>Pryor connected with fellow senior Gavin Tillman on a 26-yard TD to open the scoring. Lindblom led 28-0 until South Shore’s Zhyare Harris scored on a 16-yard run halfway through the fourth quarter.</p><p>“[Pryor and I] have been working since the start of freshman year, practicing with each other and building chemistry,” Tillman said. “Not only me and him but all of the receivers.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: 'There's no lead safe from Caleb,' but Bears want Williams lighting up red zone early, too
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Before he walked off the field after a hot — and heated — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/27/bears-training-camp-report-no-20-dt-gervon-dexter-hamstring-not-with-team-in-tennessee" target="_blank" >joint practice</a>, Titans coach Robert Saleh wanted to talk to Ben Johnson about his quarterback, Caleb Williams.</p><p>“Just telling him like, he’s like a modern-day — and I don’t wanna compare the two — Russell Wilson,” Saleh said Thursday, invoking the recently retired former Seahawks star. “When it got to the fourth quarter you better be up three scores. There’s no lead safe from Caleb.”</p><p>In his 14-year career, Wilson led his teams on 32 regular-season fourth-quarter comebacks — and four in the postseason. Williams led all quarterbacks last season with six regular-season fourth quarter comebacks — and added another in the first round against the Packers for good measure. Only three of those came in the red zone, though, and only one in the red zone was a pass.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> want Williams to get better in the red zone. As training camp wound to a close Thursday, Johnson said he was excited about exactly that.</p><p>“I think that’s been probably the best thing so far this camp,” Johnson said. “Just the anticipation, the timing, the understanding of where we want to put the football.</p><p>“He is not afraid to fit it into tight windows. He trusts his pass catchers.”</p><p>That wasn’t the case at this time last year, when Williams was more focused on learning the playbook from his new head coach.</p><p>“A year ago, I think a lot of the things we’re foreign to him,” Johnson said. “And now you can tell he has some banked reps and he’s able to anticipate where he wants to go with the football.”</p><p>Williams pushed back when asked whether he was processing the coverage better. If anything, he said, he’s benefited from an increased knowledge of what the Bears are doing — not the defense.</p><p>“I think it’s just understanding the play better, the plays that we’ve put in,” he said. “And then not having necessarily to relearn plays …</p><p>“Coach can add in more detail. Coach can add in more plays.”</p><p>That trust is paramount — and the reason why, when asked to give advice to Titans quarterback Cam Ward — a fellow No. 1 overall pick — Williams focused on the play-caller. Former Giants head coach Brian Daboll, the new Titans coordinator, has developed quarterbacks throughout his career.</p><p>“Just believing and trusting in him,” Williams said, “and what he's coaching you and teaching you.”</p><p>Ward said he’s watched film of Williams last year to try to learn how he could grow in the same way. He’s talked to Williams, too. Their dads are even friends.</p><p>“We both go through different situations, different types of adversity, whether it be early or late,” Ward said.</p><p>Williams has been a lot better late in games than early.</p><p>Williams and the Bears scored touchdowns on 57% of their red zone trips, which was tied for 14th-best but still far off of the Eagles’ league-leading 70%. Johnson has big goals — he tells his team he wants to have the highest-scoring offense of all time. To get anywhere near there, the Bears need to be more efficient inside the 20.</p><p>Williams needs to be more accurate in an area where the throwing lanes become more condensed. Last year, he had the second-worst completion percentage on passes or 10 yards or fewer and the fifth-worst mark on passes from 11-20 yards.</p><p>To improve that accuracy, Williams has focused on three things: his footwork, his rhythm and finding a smooth way to get his pass-catchers the ball. He has plenty of them, too — Rome Odunze, Luther Burden and Colston Loveland form one of the toughest trios in the league to try to box out on defense.</p><p>The Bears spent this week focusing on situational work — such as red zone and two-minute drills — and how to find Williams quick answers for recognizing coverage. Thursday's joint practice limited Williams’ red zone work, though he did some in seven-on-seven drills.</p><p>A red-zone focus will continue well into the season.</p><p>“There is no end line here,” Johnson said. “This is a continual process that we started well over a year ago now and we’re just continuing to build on things that we see that he’s doing well — and things that we feel he can get better at. … </p><p>"We’ll get through this block and sit down and reassess where we’re at and what we need to focus on going forward.”</p><p>Saleh said he’s been impressed by the difference Williams' time with Johnson has made</p><p>“He’s an unbelievable quarterback,” Saleh said. “He’s unique off-schedule. He can play. He can do it all. The amount of growth he’s had the past year and a half has been amazing.”</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: U.S. House committee reviewing whether CPS policies that support transgender students violate federal law
entries.summary: <p>The U.S. House Committee on Education and the Workforce is demanding Chicago Public Schools turn over a long list of documents, including complaints from parents and coaches about policies that support transgender students, as Republican members of Congress continue to look into whether the school district’s policies violate federal law.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://edworkforce.house.gov/uploadedfiles/letter_to_chicago_public_schools_from_chairman_walberg.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>In a letter sent Thursday</u></a> to Supt. Macquline King, U.S. Rep. Tim Walberg says the committee is reviewing “how CPS policies affect the safety, privacy, and well-being of children, and whether parents are excluded from major decisions involving their children.” He gave CPS until Sept. 11 to comply.</p><p>Walberg, who chairs the committee, wrote that the committee will evaluate whether CPS is violating the federal law that gives parents the right to review their child’s education records.</p><p>He also wants to see evidence that CPS has changed its policies to comply with a <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/docket/docketfiles/html/public/25a810.html" target="_blank" ><u>Supreme Court decision</u></a> that found teachers shouldn’t be prevented from disclosing information to parents if their child is transitioning their gender identity at school, such as by asking to be called by a different name.</p><p>CPS officials confirmed that they have received the letter, but offered no other statement.</p><p>The inquiry is one of several initiated by President Donald Trump’s administration into CPS policies, but so far not much has come from these investigations.</p><p>In one high-profile example, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/09/25/trump-administration-pulls-millions-in-funding-from-chicago-public-schools" target="_blank" ><u>Trump officials withheld some grant money</u></a> from CPS because they said the district’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/02/21/chicago-public-schools-black-student-success-plan-hit-with-federal-legal-challenge" target="_blank" ><u>Black Student Success Plan violated</u></a> the civil rights of students who aren’t Black. CPS sued and, <a class="Link" href="https://news.bloomberglaw.com/business-and-practice/education-department-settles-suit-over-chicago-school-grant-cuts" target="_blank" ><u>according to reporting in Bloomberg Law</u></a>, the Department of Education agreed to release the funds in a recent settlement.</p><p>Walberg did not threaten the district’s funding in his Thursday letter, but rather said the committee is looking into whether laws need to be changed. But the <a class="Link" href="https://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-education-reminds-schools-of-their-obligation-comply-parental-rights-law" target="_blank" ><u>Education Department said Wednesday</u></a> that school districts could lose federal funding <a class="Link" href="https://studentprivacy.ed.gov/sites/default/files/resource_document/file/SPPO%20Back%20to%20School%20DCL_August2026_Final508.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>if they failed to disclose plans</u></a> or other information about a child’s gender identity to a parent who requests to see it.</p><p>Walberg’s letter comes a few months after <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/06/10/what-to-know-as-cps-ceo-macquline-king-prepares-to-testify-before-congress-under-subpoena" target="_blank" ><u>King was forced to testify in June before the House committee</u></a>, where she faced numerous questions about CPS’ policies aimed at protecting transgender students.</p><p>Walberg references that testimony in Thursday’s letter. He wrote that King responded to a question about CPS “socially transitioning children without parental knowledge or consent” by saying that CPS does “not hide information from parents.”</p><p>But he wrote that “several of CPS’s policies and resources suggest otherwise.”</p><p>Walberg pointed to interim guidelines and a district “toolkit” that says teachers don’t need parental consent to use students’ “affirmed names and pronouns” and directs staff not to disclose a student’s “preferred name, pronoun or other confidential information pertaining to the student’s transgender or gender nonconforming status without the student’s permission.”</p><p>Walberg also takes her to task for not directly answering a question about whether CPS changed its policy to align with a recent Supreme Court ruling.</p><p>“CPS’s policies appear to undermine the authority of parents and guardians,” he writes, noting the Supreme Court has stated parents “have primary authority with respect to ‘the upbringing and education of children.’”</p><p>Walberg requests that CPS send the committee red-lined copies of guidelines that show how they’ve changed their policies following the Supreme Court decision, as well as a description of training provided to staff “on the topics of gender and sexuality, including transgender, nonbinary, gender nonconforming, and LGBTQ+.”</p><p>CPS was one of the first districts to implement specific policies supporting “gender diversity.” In Chicago, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/06/09/chicago-public-schools-ceo-macquline-king-heading-to-dc-hearing-transgender-and-black-students" target="_blank" ><u>those policies have not drawn much controversy</u></a>. Students and parents have advocated for them when they were up for debate, rather than complaining about them.</p>

entries.title: Car passenger, CPD officer hospitalized after Garfield Ridge crash
entries.summary: <p>Two people, including a Chicago police officer, were hospitalized after a crash Thursday afternoon in Garfield Ridge, according to police.</p><p>An officer in an unmarked squad car was traveling southbound in the 6400 block of West Archer Avenue at 4:39 p.m. when the vehicle was struck near a parking lot by a 38-year-old man driving a sedan, police said.</p><p>The officer was taken to a nearby hospital in fair condition with a neck injury.</p><p>A passenger in the sedan, a 36-year-old woman, was taken to MacNeal Hospital in fair condition with right arm and leg injuries, police said. The driver of the sedan declined medical attention.</p><p>No citations were issued.</p>

entries.title: Chicago murals: Caleb Williams' pose from the Madden NFL 27 cover gives the Bears QB a big West Loop presence
entries.summary: <p>A 25-foot tall image of Bears quarterback Caleb Williams gave Chicago artist Asend the opportunity to flex his knack for fine art details and his graffiti writer style in a massive mural for the West Loop that Bears fans are stopping to see in person.</p><p>Completed earlier this month, the three-story image stretches 35 feet wide and features the image of Williams in his “Iceman” pose, with arms crossed across his chest, in front of a navy blue wall. The mural is on the Halsted Street side of La Josie, a Mexican restaurant off the busy Randolph Street corridor. Williams' nails are painted in Bears’ orange and blue. The image mirrors the cover of the Madden NFL 27 video game.</p><p>Asend added his own touch behind Williams. Friends familiar with his graffiti style recognized his lettering font, as “The Chicago Bears” wording flanks Williams’ football helmet with paint drops from the letters seeming to run down the wall. Football play diagrams, with their Xs, Os and arrows, are in each quadrant. The lettering and the plays are in orange, and all of it pops from the blue behind it.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The mural was sponsored by the Bears and EA Sports, the maker of the Madden game, Asend says.</p><p>“They gave me artistic freedom to create the background for this Madden cover mural and give it a local touch with a little bit of energy and a little bit of spice,” he says.</p><p>The mural also was meaningful because the Bears are a team that unites the city, Asend says. There’s no North Side, South Side, West Side: “The Bears are the glue for everyone.”</p><p>“After the success and excitement that the Bears had last year, we’re still riding that high, right? Let’s go. It’s perfect timing for preseason to get back on that energy that we left off with.”</p><p>The details of the painting, particularly the folds in the jersey and the way the light hits them, also play into what Asend has explored in the studio in recent years. While he started as a graffiti writer and is known for his murals, he has a thriving studio practice. Asend also hosts residencies around the world to help artists develop their business savvy while taking elevating their work.</p><p>Asend murals can be found around Chicago and Highwood, where his <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DCEzBu-J0R4/" target="_blank" >image of a graffiti writer walking away from a freshly tagged Metra train</a> can be spotted on the Highwood Historical Society building.</p><p>Saida Rodriguez-Guerrero, Chicago Bears manager of fan development and brand marketing, says the timing was perfect for the Williams mural.</p><p>“It bridges sports, art and community, and I think everyone was super excited to come together and celebrate a really exciting time for the team.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d00000" name="module-d00000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Murals and Mosaics Newsletter</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-990000" name="html-embed-module-990000"></a><div class="piano-sidebar-newsletter-murals-and-mosaics"></div> </div> </div></div> </div><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b20000" name="module-b20000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Chicago’s murals and mosaics sidebar</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals-mosaics" target="_blank" >Chicago’s murals & mosaics</a></h3>Part of a series on public art in the city and suburbs. <b>Know of a mural or mosaic? entries.title: Boy, 16, among 3 teens shot including his brother on West Side, dies
entries.summary: <p>A 16-year-old boy who was among three teens shot — including his 18-year-old brother — after attending a barbecue in the Austin neighborhood last week has died, officials said.</p><p>Cortez Hall, an Austin High School student, died at 10:32 p.m. Thursday at Mount Sinai Hospital, according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office and a Chicago police report. An autopsy is scheduled. </p><p>Hall and the other two teens were shot <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/18/2-teens-critically-injured-in-south-austin-drive-by-shooting" target="_blank" >Aug. 18 about 9:30 p.m.</a> after they’d left a front yard barbecue in the 5500 block of West Quincy Street, police and the medical examiner’s office said.</p><p>After walking west to the 200 block of South Central Avenue, four assailants began shooting after jumping out of two vehicles that had stopped directly east of them, according to a police report.</p><p>The 18-year-old was shot in his right side and Hall was shot in the chest, shoulder and right leg, police said. The siblings were initially in critical condition - both at Mount Sinai.</p><p>Another 16-year-old boy, who was found by officers at the scene with a graze wound to his arm and refused medical attention, police said.</p><p>The assailants sped away north on Central and were not arrested, according to the report.</p><p>No arrests have been reported. </p><p>Detectives are investigating. <br></p>

entries.title: Woman, 67, shot in Roseland
entries.summary: <p>A woman is recovering a a hospital after being shot in the leg early Friday in the Roseland neighborhood. </p><p>The woman, 67, noticed two people near a parked car around 5:45 a.m. in the 9300 block of South Stewart Avenue and approached them when they opened fire and struck her in the leg, Chicago police said. </p><p>She was taken to the Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn where her condition was stabilized, police said. </p><p>Area 2 detectives were investigating. </p>

property tax discounts, Cook County made him pay. Then, it renewed them.</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-ydnhuil-l-d/" target="_blank" >Tim Novak</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-ydnhuil-l-h/" target="_blank" >Keenan Chen</a></h5><p><b>Non-senior discount</b>: Armando W. Saleh, a former Cook County employee turned lobbyist, got more than $20,000 in property tax breaks meant for low-income senior citizens — even though voting records and other government documents say he's 56 years old. How? Saleh submitted a passport to the Cook County assessor's office that showed him as being 15 years older, according to a Sun-Times investigation of the government office.</p><p><b>Breaks secured</b>: The passport, issued in March 2021, was among many documents used by Saleh, an ex-chief of staff to a Cook County commissioner, to secure 69 tax breaks that saved him a total of more than $80,000 under Assessor Fritz Kaegi and two predecessors going back to 1998.</p><p><b>How'd this happen?</b>: It's unclear why the three assessors kept approving tax breaks on Saleh’s two homes despite a state law that limits those exemptions to just one, an owner-occupied home.</p><p><b>Watchdogs investigations</b>: Saleh is now the latest of more than a dozen homeowners who have lost their tax breaks following Sun-Times investigations of the county office.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-ydnhuil-l-k/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>GRAVE href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-ydnhuil-l-o/" target="_blank" >Sisters have cremated remains and doubt, wondering, ‘Where is my mama?’</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-ydnhuil-l-b/" target="_blank" >Cindy Hernandez</a></h5><p><b>Chilling discovery</b>: When sisters Franquella and Marshawna Campbell learned that Clark Morgan, the man who had picked up their mother's body from hospice, had been accused of mishandling human remains, they turned to the urn sitting on the table in their mother’s living room. They opened it and began to question everything, including whether the urn's contents are ashes at all.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-ydnhuil-l-n/" target="_blank" >state shut down</a> South Chicago Chapel this month after receiving a tip that owners Clark and Johanna Morgan were improperly storing bodies. Inside the funeral home, investigators found 56 bodies in various stages of decomposition. Last year, a Chicago Heights Crematory, owned by the Morgans, was shut down.</p><p><b>Search for answers</b>: Most of the bodies have been identified, and families have been notified, but the Campbells might never get that call. When they visited the Cook County medical examiner's office to ask whether their mother was among the bodies recovered from South Chicago Chapel, officials told them they were still working to identify the remains. The sisters want what's inside their mother's urn tested, but the medical examiner's office said they don't have the tools to test cremains.</p><p><a class="Link" target="_blank" >More than 200 tornadoes have hit Illinois this year. The reason why is unclear.</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-ydnhuil-l-c/" target="_blank" >Juanpablo Ramirez-Franco</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-ydnhuil-l-q/" target="_blank" >Matt Simon</a></h5><p><b>Tornado tally</b>: So far this year, 207 tornadoes and counting have touched down in Illinois. That figure may rise as officials continue working through the remaining post-storm assessments, according to the National Weather Service. This is the third year in a row that Illinois has experienced a triple-digit tornado season; the state's historical average is closer to 50.</p><p><b>Research continue</b>s: Experts agree it doesn't seem that climate change is in and of itself resulting in more tornadoes. If that seems unsatisfyingly inconclusive, it's not for lack of trying. Tornadoes are hyperlocal weather events, so they’re difficult to simulate in climate models. Massive hurricanes, on the other hand, are easier to model. So scientists are still working to figure out how much the change in tornado activity is due to natural variability — what you'd expect if humans hadn't warmed the planet — versus what's the consequence of runaway greenhouse gas emissions.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-ydnhuil-l-a/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>MORE NEWS YOU on a mission to bring goodwill to Chicago's hip-hop community.</p><p>The new multiday music festival and conference kicks off Friday with two days of panels and networking at Venue Six10, featuring talks with rappers Killer Mike and Vic Mensa as well as writing sessions with Brother Ali and Phenom.</p><p>It will be followed by an all-day festival Sunday at Salt Shed, headlined by Killer Mike, entries.title: Pedestrian fatally struck in Dan Ryan hit-and-run
entries.summary: <p>A pedestrian standing next to their apparently disabled vehicle was fatally struck in a hit and run that temporarily shut down local lanes of the Dan Ryan Expressway early Friday on the South Side. </p><p>State troopers responded to the local lanes near 47th Street around 2:40 a.m. where a person standing next to their stopped vehicle on the left shoulder was struck by a vehicle that fled the scene, Illinois state police said. </p><p>The person was taken to an area hospital where they died, state police said. </p><p>Local inbound lanes of I-94 were shut down and traffic was diverted at 55th Street, officials said. Lanes reopened around 5:35 a.m.</p>

entries.title: Loretto Hospital's indicted former CFO is in federal custody in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Loretto Hospital’s indicted<b> </b>former chief financial officer<b> </b>has returned to the United States and is being held in Chicago’s federal jail, arriving just as a new grand jury<b> </b>accused him of scamming<b> </b>the federal government<b> </b>out of roughly<b> </b>$200 million, the Chicago Sun-Times has confirmed.</p><p>Anosh<b> </b>Ahmed<b> </b>may now try to take advantage of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >months-long scandal</a> in the office of U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros<b> </b>to try to have his charges thrown out. No such motion has been filed, but Ahmed is set to be arraigned on the new indictment Monday morning.</p><p>The feds will likely use the new indictment against Ahmed to avoid that outcome. It was handed up Thursday, secured in an effort to replace a set of previously tainted charges. But the judge presiding over the case <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/10/hearing-in-loretto-hospital-case-could-address-claims-of-prosecutors-misconduct-if-feds-dont-drop-it" target="_blank" >is clearly bothered</a> by the scandal, which involves misconduct before grand jurors. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/29/loretto-hospital-fraud-anosh-ahmed-broadview-six" >Indicted ex-Loretto exec’s return to U.S. could add to feds’ ‘Broadview 6' headaches</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Ahmed, 42, is being held in the Metropolitan Correctional Center, records show. He's been under indictment in Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/07/12/loretto-hospital-cfo-15-million-embezzlement" target="_blank" >since 2024</a>, when he was originally accused of scheming with others<b> </b>to embezzle more than $15 million<b> </b>out of the safety net hospital on Chicago’s West Side. Those charges are still pending.</p><p>Then, in 2025, a grand jury handed up an indictment<b> </b>accusing him of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/06/17/former-loretto-hospital-executive-charged-fake-covid-testing-scheme" target="_blank" >COVID-19 testing scheme</a> that defrauded<b> </b>the federal government<b> </b>out of hundreds of millions of dollars.</p><p>The probe of Ahmed and Loretto Hospital dates back to 2021, when Block Club Chicago reported the hospital had shared COVID-19 vaccines with employees at Trump Tower, where Ahmed had a condo. The vaccines were just becoming available and were still rare.</p><p>Six people were charged along with Ahmed<b> </b>in the two separate cases. Meanwhile, Ahmed left Chicago for France and Dubai<b> </b>in August 2023 after he became aware of the investigation, federal prosecutors have said. He was taken into custody<b> </b>in Serbia<b> </b>last November.</p><p>His attorneys denied he was a fugitive, saying his return to the United States was delayed because of “several significant family health issues.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/26/defense-attorney-wants-broadview-6-prosecutor-on-the-stand-in-cbp-sex-assault-case-she-hasnt-testified" >Defense attorney wants ‘Broadview 6' prosecutor on the stand in CBP sex assault case: ‘She hasn’t testified’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Meanwhile, the cases against his co-defendants began to collapse this summer following <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >revelations of prosecutor misconduct</a> involving the “Broadview Six,”<b> </b>a group of Operation Midway Blitz protesters accused of a conspiracy<b> </b>to impede a federal officer.</p><p>Boutros dropped the charges against the “Broadview Six” after a judge revealed<b> </b>that Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri Mecklenburg<b> </b>acted improperly before the grand jury.</p><p>Mecklenburg also handled the cases against Ahmed and his co-defendants, and she’s since been accused of similar wrongdoing in that prosecution.</p><p>No hearing has been held over the allegations against Mecklenburg, a point of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/26/defense-attorney-wants-broadview-6-prosecutor-on-the-stand-in-cbp-sex-assault-case-she-hasnt-testified" target="_blank" >growing frustration</a> in the legal community.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Sharon Johnson Coleman presides over the case brought against Ahmed in 2025. She threatened in June<b> </b>to hold a hearing<b> </b>over the Mecklenburg scandal. That hearing likely would have seen Boutros summoned to the witness stand, in addition to Mecklenburg.</p><p>Boutros’ office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" target="_blank" >avoided the hearing</a> by quickly — and permanently — dropping criminal charges against two of Ahmed’s co-defendants. The feds have since worked to strike deals with the remaining four.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" >After judge threatens hearing over grand jury misconduct, feds drop charges in case tied to Loretto exec</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But when Ahmed’s lawyers sought similar relief, Coleman said<b> </b>he’d first have to be “arraigned, in-person, before this court.”</p><p>The news that he’d agreed to return to the United States came about two weeks later.</p><p>Former U.S. Attorney Dan Webb and others from the Winston Taylor LLP law firm have filed appearances on Ahmed’s behalf in recent days. But they’ve yet to file a new motion for dismissal.</p><p>If Coleman agrees to a hearing, Boutros’ office could face a critical decision: Drop charges against a man accused of scheming hundreds of millions out of the federal government, or go forward with the hearing even after it permanently dropped charges in an apparent effort to avoid it.</p><p>The feds will likely argue any taint from Mecklenburg was cured when they secured a new indictment against Ahmed. But Coleman is clearly interested in getting to the bottom of what’s been going on in the U.S. attorney’s office.</p><p>She<b> </b>warned prosecutors in June that a hearing was “still a possibility.”</p><p>“I’m not saying that’s over with,” she said.</p>
entries.author: Jon Seidel

entries.title: Dear Abby: Metronome Man Bounces Between Two Wives
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Twenty-six years ago, I began what was supposed to be an affair with my current girlfriend, "Lacey." I was married at the time, and when my then-wife caught me, I was told we needed only to figure out who got what out of the marriage. Believing there was no salvaging the marriage, I took what was available and stayed with Lacey.</p><p>My ex-wife moved on, and we divorced. Lacey got pregnant. After the birth of our daughter, and having become "Dad" to Lacey's other two children, I stayed. The biological father of Lacey's young children was deceased, so I raised them as my own, the same as my biological child.</p><p>Now, after years of regret about screwing up my marriage, I mustered the courage to contact my ex-wife via social media. We connected via a messenger app for a few days. After those conversations went extremely well, we eventually exchanged numbers. There were lots of truths told, some good, some bad, but all in complete honesty. The conversations have been emotional and uplifting. I feel happy thinking about her and hope someday to see her again in person.</p><p>I have been unhappy with Lacey since the beginning, always regretting the screwup I made in losing my first wife. Now, speaking to her again, I feel motivated to leave Lacey. There seems to be an honest connection with my ex, and we both hint at rekindling the relationship. How do I broach this subject civilly with Lacey without ruining my relationships with all of my kids? — <i>SORRY IN PENNSYLVANIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR SORRY:</b> Do not expect a civil conversation. Expect instead that Lacey will be angry, threatened and furious. It may cushion the blow to mention that you haven't been happy for years, and that you will see that she is provided for financially in some way. (Discuss this with a lawyer beforehand.)</p><p>Explain to your grown children that you have not been happy for many years, but because you love them, you stayed with their mom until they were all adults so their lives would not be disrupted. If you do this gently and reasonably, they may listen.</p><p>A word to the wise: There is no guarantee that returning to your ex-wife will bring you the happiness you are expecting. Premarital counseling and a long courtship are essential to ensure you aren't jumping from the fire back into the frying pan.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My boyfriend, "Ted," is divorced from a woman who now has Alzheimer's. Ted has been the only one to step up to help her through this difficult time. It takes a lot of his time and effort and weighs heavily on his mind.</p><p>I admire Ted for his loyalty to someone he once shared a life with, but now she wants him to go on a cruise with her and a couple of his relatives. Ted says she doesn't get to travel much now, and he sees nothing wrong with this because she's paying his way. I am not invited. I feel this goes above and beyond his involvement with her health management. When is enough enough? — <i>SECOND FIDDLE</i></p><p><b>DEAR SECOND FIDDLE:</b> Ted's kindness is admirable, but his willingness to set you aside and vacation with his ex-wife crosses a line. Tell him either you accompany him on the cruise, or he shouldn't bother coming back from it.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned the column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Trump, his lackeys will try to steal 2026 elections
entries.summary: <p>The Supreme Court gave us a start this week, with what looked, at first glance, like a win for Donald Trump's efforts to suppress mail-in ballots. But, as Andrew Egger explained, that isn't quite what happened. In broad outline, the Court stayed a lower court injunction while the legality of Trump's attempted interference will be decided later. It was a temporary, procedural win for Trump, but not a permission slip.</p><p>Not yet, anyway. After the 2024 immunity ruling, you'd be ill-advised to assume anything about this Court. Until three years ago, it was axiomatic that the president was not above the law. The Roberts Court undermined that key principle. And here, too, it seems an open-and-shut case that the Constitution grants power over elections to the Congress and the states, not to the executive branch. But we'll see.</p><p>Still, the Court's little summer fright is a good reminder that early voting will begin in some places in as little as four weeks, and while the polls and projections look good for Democrats, this is not an ordinary election year. Trump is weakened and flailing, yes, but he remains determined to prevent a free and fair election in November if he possibly can. And he does not lack for lackeys.</p><p>The Supreme Court touched on just one of his efforts to subvert the election: his executive order directing the Postal Service to work with states to determine whether voters requesting mail-in ballots were citizens.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b70000" name="module-b70000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>There have been other below-the-radar efforts to subvert election security. Since 2025, the Justice Department has demanded voter rolls from 48 states. Nearly all states are resisting, and the matter is in litigation. Recall that after immigration officers shot and killed Alex Pretti in Minneapolis and feelings were running high, the administration didn't express regret or apologize. Nor did they announce an investigation. Instead, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi sent Gov. Tim Walz a letter offering to suspend Operation Metro Surge if Minnesota agreed to end its sanctuary city policies and hand over its voter registration rolls and Medicaid and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, enrollees' names and addresses. And here you thought the Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids were all about finding the "worst of the worst."</p><p>Christopher Krebs, director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency in Trump's first term, became a target of his wrath because he truthfully testified that the 2020 election was free and fair. In the second term, Trump has gutted the agency Krebs had helmed, denying to states and the federal government key tools to detect foreign election interference. Strange priority for someone who is so consumed with anger at the accusation that he benefited from Russian interference in the 2016 election.</p><p>In July, the president announced a major primetime address that would contain a "bombshell" and then rambled incoherently for what seemed like hours about an "unprecedented election security nightmare." It was China, he claimed, that had actually intervened in the 2020 election. The speech was immediately forgotten, but perhaps it ought not to be. Trump rarely gives primetime speeches. He may have been preparing the ground for some declaration to come.</p><p>Meanwhile, Trump instructed Republicans in red states to engage in naked, midcycle gerrymandering. There was no pretense that this was an effort to respond to Democratic gerrymandering. Several states with Democratic majorities like California and Virginia had recently taken steps to limit partisan gerrymandering. Regarding Texas, which was the first state to salute smartly and carry out Trump's wishes, Trump said: "Just a simple redrawing; we pick up five seats."</p><p>What else could be in store?</p><p>Trump has never ruled out using force to affect the election outcome. He attempted it with the Capitol mob in 2021, and even in the past year and a half, he has expressed regret that he didn't take Lt. Gen. Michael Flynn's advice and use troops to confiscate every voting machine in the country in 2020. Asked in May whether he would consider using the National Guard or ICE to patrol polling places, he said, "I'd do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections."</p><p>In February of this year, he told talk show host (and former deputy director of the FBI) Dan Bongino that Republicans "should take over the voting in at least many -- 15 places. The Republicans ought to nationalize the voting." And in a meeting with Volodymyr Zelensky, Trump mused that we might pause our elections "if we happen to be in a war with somebody."</p><p>Trump's factotums have also signaled a certain insouciance about the possibility of sending armed officers to polling places. At his confirmation hearing, Todd Blanche asked: "Why is there an objection to sending ICE to polling stations? Illegals can't vote. It doesn't make any sense."</p><h3>ICE threats at the polls </h3><p>Feigned confusion to one side, Blanche knows exactly why sending ICE to polling places would be outrageous. After a two-year spree of arrests, manhandling, family separations, detentions, deportations and even executions of Hispanic-looking people and others, it would be completely understandable that Hispanic citizens might hesitate to exercise their right to vote if they feared being wrongly caught up in an ICE enforcement action. No fewer than 170 American citizens have been stopped, arrested and detained for days, sometimes in gruesome conditions. In fact, even non-Hispanic Americans would have reason to fear: Neither Renee Good nor Pretti was Hispanic.</p><p>Despite their best efforts to hire poorly qualified recruits, ICE still lacks the numbers to perform any kind of nationwide patrol of polling places. There are roughly 95,000 polling places across the country, but at most, ICE might muster 10,000 to 15,000 officers. In key districts, though, that could make a difference. It's illegal under several statutes to "intimidate, threaten, or coerce" any person "for the purpose of interfering with their right to vote." But Trump might tell his minions to ignore the law, promising pardons later.</p><p>Finally, there is always the possibility that Trump may declare some sort of emergency and attempt to use his powers under the Insurrection Act to federalize the National Guard and deploy them to polling places to supplement ICE. They may calculate that this usurpation would be declared illegal later — but later would be fine if turnout in Democratic areas could be suppressed.</p><p>There's another possibility, too, that would require more coordination among Republicans willing to do anything for Trump — but we've seen that kind of destructive devotion before. If governors and secretaries of state in the right combination of states find reason-however flimsy or farcical — to avoid certifying November's vote by the time Congress convenes on Jan. 3, it's possible that the rump House that assembles could have a Republican "majority." That "majority" could elect a speaker, and that speaker could thereafter delay seating rightfully elected Democrats even after their elections are certified, as Speaker Mike Johnson did for many weeks after a special election in 2025.</p><p>The GOP is the party that failed to certify Joe Biden's victory. Nothing should be considered inconceivable.</p><p>It's in our hands. Protect Democracy, the American Civil Liberties Union, the Brennan Center for Justice and many others are preparing for whatever may come. Protect Democracy offers guidance on your local elections with state-by-state rules. Know the law. Be prepared. Volunteer at a polling place. Take nothing for granted. There is no bottom with MAGA.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of the Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f80000" name="module-f80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Young police officers, as I once was, don't have all the answers
entries.summary: <p>Every few months, police academies graduate new officers. At first glance, these young officers seem to know everything. But looking prepared and being experienced are two different things. </p><p>I learned that early, when what should have been a routine arrest turned into a trip to the emergency room, a series of shots and one of the most embarrassing moments of my career. </p><p>I don’t recall why I arrested this person, only that it was a misdemeanor — something like public drinking or trespassing. After completing the paperwork, I returned to the street, only to be called back by the lock-up officer. When officers get a call from the lock-up, their first thought is "What did I do wrong?" The worst-case scenario was that I missed a weapon during the search, or illegal drugs were found on the person afterward. </p><p>The good news was that I didn’t do anything wrong; the bad news was that the arrestee claimed to have hepatitis B, which sent me to the emergency room. There, as a precautionary measure, I was immediately given a shot; one month later, another, and finally, another as the final booster to ensure long-term, lifelong protection. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3f0000" name="module-3f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>A few weeks later, I arrived at the defendant's court hearing. As I looked around the courtroom, I noticed the assistant public defender handling the case was noticeably pregnant. When the judge sat on the bench and began calling cases, the assistant public defender called her clients and directed them to the hallway for pretrial preparation. When she came around to call my arrestee, panic set in. I felt anxious because she was obviously unaware that he had hepatitis B. </p><p>To be clear, hepatitis B isn't transmitted though <a class="Link" href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/hepatitis-b/symptoms-causes/syc-20366802" target="_blank" >casual contact</a>. But I thought the assistant public defender should be aware of her client's health since I had been sent to the hospital following the arrest.</p><p>There was an unwritten rule, or at least one I had quickly picked up as a young officer: Police officers and assistant public defenders were not supposed to be friends. You kept your distance. I didn't want to be seen talking to her, and I was sure she felt the same way. So I pivoted toward the prosecutors' table and asked a prosecutors to inform the defense attorney about her client's hepatitis B. The assistant state's attorney assured me he would, but he left the courtroom without informing the assistant public defender. </p><p>As the judge continued hearing cases, I jumped up when I saw the assistant public defender heading toward the hallway. "Officer, if you have something to say to me, go talk to the prosecutor!" she said loudly enough that everyone in the courtroom turned to look. Embarrassed and now angry, I walked over and told her, quietly that her client had hepatitis B.</p><p>The bewildered judge could only say, "Everything OK, officer?" I snapped back, "Yes, everything is just fine." I sat there steaming, convinced I had just embarrassed myself in front of an entire courtroom. A few minutes later, the assistant public defender sat down beside me. She thanked me, and I wished her and her baby well.</p><p>That day I learned I didn't have to get so worked up and that assistant public defenders, like all other members of the community, can be friendly to police officers, in spite of what I was told. </p><h3>Knowledge comes with experience </h3><p>Police academies are not designed to teach police culture or the unwritten rules. Those are absorbed through courtroom culture, squad room conversations and years of watching how things actually work. Over time, I learned to exchange subtle nods in the hallways, stay professional and keep my distance on active and inactive cases. Nobody taught me that. Experience did. </p><p>The academy gives recruits knowledge. Experience, mentorship and time turn that knowledge into judgment. The public sees the badge and assumes that officer has both. Often, they have only the first.</p><p>In other professions, inexperience is often visible. Medical residents work under attending physicians. New pilots spend years under the supervision of experienced captains. But when a rookie police officer steps out of a squad car, no sign tells the public this may be their third month on the job. The badge looks the same.</p><p>Before they become veterans, they will eventually find themselves in a situation they were trained for, only to discover that real life has introduced something the academy could not have anticipated. A detail. A person. An emotion. A decision with no clear answer. And somewhere in the back of their minds will be the same question I once had: "Now what the heck do I do?"</p><p><i>Louis Martinez is a professor of law enforcement at Oakton College’s Des Plaines campus and a former Chicago Police Department officer. He has written about law enforcement issues for nearly two decades.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f90000" name="module-f90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: Louis Martinez

entries.title: Gary's power debacle is an ominous sign for Bears' Indiana stadium
entries.summary: <p>Are Bears brass watching the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/morning-edition/2026/08/24/gary-northwest-indiana-chicago-public-schools-cook-county-property-taxes" >debacle</a> unfold in Indiana as they contemplate building a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/13/bears-stadium-update-hammond-arlington-heights-george-mccaskey-kevin-warren-chairman-president-indiana-illinois-nfl" >stadium in Hammond</a>?</p><p>For two weeks following an Aug. 11 storm, Indiana officials were scrambling to restart power for most residents in Gary, the second-most populous city in Northwest Indiana. Residents didn't have energy as food and medicine in refrigerators rotted, supermarkets and pharmacies lacked power and lawsuits against the local utility company were being prepared.</p><p>The irony is rich as the Bears are threatening to cross state lines in part because of infrastructure funding for their proposed stadium in Illinois.</p><p>Crews from ComEd — the utility in scary, “dysfunctional” northern Illinois — provided support to Indiana to restore power. It’s unlikely <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/28/chicago-bears-hammond-hams-escalating-rhetoric-hoosiers-hope-bears-stadium" >Hoosiers officials</a> who love to attack Illinois to prop up their careers are eating crow. Humility is grounded in truth.<br>  <br><i>Craig Barner, Lincoln Square</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a60000" name="module-a60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Football first </h3><p>Perhaps if the residents of Gary told Indiana Gov. Mike Braun they had a football team, he might have been more motivated to help them.</p><p><i>Don Anderson, Oak Park</i></p><h3>FEMA, give Gary more aid </h3><p>We had a sizable portion of Indiana without power for two weeks. So why hasn't the Federal Emergency Management Agency issue a major disaster declaration? Indiana voted for Donald Trump, so why not more help? </p><p><i>Marcelline Ricker, Downers Grove</i></p><h3></h3><h3>Murdered victims’ families’ hopelessness</h3><p>It's been 34 years since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/23/person-of-interest-1992-kidnapping-murder-tammy-zywicki-isp-fbi" >Tammy Zywicki</a>, 20, was murdered. Her case remains unsolved. My 20-year-old brother <a class="Link" href="https://www.dupagesheriff.org/unsolvedMurders" target="_blank" >Roger was murdered</a> in in DuPage County 1974. His case also remains unsolved. </p><p>How murder affects the victim's families is impossible to describe or explain. It literally changes your perspective on everything. Emotionally, you're never the same. It's unconscionable to me why an omniscient God wouldn't just whisper into the ears of the investigators who the killer was and where to find the evidence for a conviction. How easy, moral and just that would be, so the bereaved can simply get a tiny measure of closure. After all, it wouldn't upset the world order in any way whatsoever. It's unforgivable. Unless of course, God doesn't exist.</p><p><i>Wes Dickson, Orland Park</i></p><h3>Dodoes with dildos </h3><p>Just when you thought the nonsense was over, the dildos are back throwing sex toys on to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/21/skys-natasha-cloud-calls-out-offenders-after-sex-toys-thrown-onto-court" >court at WNBA games</a>. Fellas, seriously, take your toys home and maybe use them in some other way. You might discover that you enjoy your dildo more than being one.</p><p><i>Paul Koehler, Rogers Park</i></p><h3>Not getting children vaccinated is a bad move</h3><p>Unproven conspiracy theories are taking effect. Vaccination percentages are <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026/aug/22/kindergarten-mmr-vaccination-rates-dip" target="_blank" >beginning to drop</a> among school-age children. Parents who are too young to remember polio, rubella and other health threats are following the suggestions of nonmedical Cabinet members and aren't vaccinating their children.</p><p>Perhaps these parents should remember what the Ghost of Christmas Present told Scrooge. The spirit <a class="Link" href="https://www.open-bks.com/library/classics/dickens_charles_carol/carol-101-102.html" target="_blank" >warns</a> Scrooge to beware of want and ignorance but states that he must fear ignorance the most.</p><p><i>Warren Rodgers Jr., Orland Park</i><br></p>

entries.title: GoodWaves fest, featuring Killer Mike and Chicago’s Recoechi, aims to spread the good word of Chicago hip-hop
entries.summary: <p>GoodWaves is on a mission to bring goodwill to Chicago’s hip-hop community.</p><p>The new multiday music festival and conference kicks off Friday with two days of panels and networking at Venue Six10, featuring talks with rappers Killer Mike and Vic Mensa as well as writing sessions with Brother Ali and Phenom. It will be followed with an all-day festival Sunday at Salt Shed, headlined by Killer Mike, with additional performances from Snow Tha Product and Rapsody, alongside up-and-coming local talents Recoechi and Pinqy Ring. The nonprofit collective <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/art/2025/08/07/mecca-flats-bronzeville-inflatable-monument-floating-museum" target="_blank" >Floating Museum</a> will also be present with three monuments.</p><p>All of the events are free (They're “sold out,” but there is a waitlist that people can sign up for online).</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div id="module-940000" name="module-940000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>GoodWaves Festival</h3><br><b>When:</b> Aug. 28-30<br><b>Where:</b> Venue SIX10, 610 S. Michigan Ave., and Salt Shed, 1357 N. Elston Ave.<br><b>Tickets:</b> Sold out, but attendees can sign up for the waitlist<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.groundwaveshiphop.com/" target="_blank" >groundwaveshiphop.com</a></div> </div><p>“I want everyone to feel welcome. No one should feel like hip-hop is alien or not safe. We’re too old for that. And we are amplifying that by taking down the barrier of having to pay to [take] part,” said organizer MURS 3:16.</p><p>The L.A.-based rapper, a leader in the underground rap scene, is staging the event as part of his Groundwaves organization, which aims to mobilize hip-hop communities around the country. The group previously engaged in similar efforts in Fort Collins, Colorado, and Tulsa, Oklahoma, where it helped establish TMC Records, the first-ever label run by students in classes at McLain High School for Science and Technology.</p><p>Last year, when MURS was approached by local artist and culture organization Good Chaos about creating programs to benefit young emcees in Chicago, he was all in. Every month, MURS flies in to host popular open mic nights at Co-Prosperity in Bridgeport, one-on-one mentorship sessions at Parkway Social in Grand Boulevard and all-ages Generations parties at the National Public Housing Museum on the Near West Side, where everyone from ages 8 months old to 85 years old has come to participate in clean rap sessions. GoodWaves brings it all together and allows more space to invite more people.</p><p>“Our goal is to solidify Chicago as the fourth pillar of the hip-hop community in the United States behind New York, Los Angeles and Atlanta,” said MURS. “When you think about Twista, Common, Lupe, Chance and Kanye, no one can argue they are five elite-level artists. And there's no other city in the world where they could come from and not have it considered an epicenter. But the industry doesn't always respect Chicago as an epicenter,” MURS said, referencing the fact that there are no major record labels and few industry launching pads in the city beyond a media brand like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/06/11/lil-uzi-vert-chief-keef-summer-smash-hip-hop-festival-cole-bennett-berto-solorio-lyrical-lemonade" target="_blank" >Lyrical Lemonade</a>.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-160000" name="image-160000"></a> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“Our goal is to solidify Chicago as the fourth pillar of the hip-hop community in the United States behind New York, Los Angeles and Atlanta,” said MURS. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Nigel Holt</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p> And one of his big takeaways was that creating actual spaces for exchange is the key. “I met all my friends at a record store, but that isn’t always the case anymore,” he said. “People in my generation are criticizing younger generations not realizing that a lot of spaces disappeared.” </p><p>Much of GoodWaves is inspired by what MURS gleaned from attending notable music conferences 30 years ago when he was coming up. One of them, the Gavin Seminar in California, is where he linked up with Killer Mike’s Run The Jewels collaborator El-P, who ended up signing MURS to his Definitive Jux label.</p><p>“We wound up at a Denny’s after the conference, and from there toured the world and put out lots of records and had a ton of fun,” MURS said. “That’s what I want to come out of GoodWaves.”</p><p>Recoechi is excited about that potential.</p><p>“Collaboration is the thing that's going to bring us together. We gotta build our community,” said the Chicago rapper who will perform at the event Sunday. “I think we lost community for a time because everybody became superstars and went to L.A. But I think people are going to witness the new era of what Chicago hip-hop is becoming … with unity among artists.” </p><p>His perspective is one of the reasons, when MURS was laying the groundwork in Chicago, Recoechi’s name kept coming up.</p><p>The rapper, who grew up on Stony Island, was inspired by Taylor Bennett to take up freestyling when he attended Urban Prep in Bronzeville in the mid-2010s. And on his just-released new album, “ACT II: Body of God,” which will also be celebrated Wednesday at Schubas, Recoechi shines a light on the power of the Chicago music community. Guest spots include Vic Mensa, J. Ivy and Saba, as well as his mentees Malik Jewelz, Rhome and Young(IN).</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>There’s also a greater sense of neighborly community that Recoechi, who works with programs including Healthy Hood Chicago, preaches in his music, too.</p><p>“I care about my people the most. I am signed by the community and want to use my platform to spread awareness,” he said.</p><p>That is music to Killer Mike’s ears. He’s another prime example of the power that can be found within the intersectionality of hip-hop and community building.</p><p>“I was an organizer before I was a rapper,” said Killer Mike, born Michael Render, who most recently launched a rent-to-own home program in his city of Atlanta. He’s carving out time from his acting duties on “The Lowdown” and “Scarpetta” and working on the follow-up to his 2023 solo album “Michael” to be part of GoodWaves, largely to honor MURS. </p><p>“He’s an underground champion and showed us that you could go your own way,” Killer Mike said.</p><p>There’s also another person he has to thank when it comes to showing him the way: Alice Johnson, a Catholic white woman who wound up working with the Atlanta Fulton Commission on Children and Youth where the two first crossed paths.</p><p>“Alice was adamant about organizing with young people, and I was one of the young people she recruited,” said Killer Mike. “She always told me you don't organize for people, you organize with people. And even when I got lucky to live out all my dreams, she was adamant about me being a mobilizer and helping. I will never forget my friend and mentor, and I will never allow her memory to be forgotten,” he added. “And I really think some of that work continues in the spirit of what MURS is doing now.”</p>

entries.title: Sisters have cremated remains and doubt, wondering, ‘Where is my mama?’
entries.summary: <p>Months ago, Shawnese Shannon’s family mourned her death and celebrated her life in a sea of purple.</p><p>She loved Prince’s “Purple Rain” and had asked her family and friends to wear her favorite color. But recently, the memory of that celebration turned to doubt and sorrow. Shannon's family is questioning whether the remains inside the urn she'd picked herself are hers and even whether the contents are ashes at all.</p><p>When sisters Franquella and Marshawna Campbell learned that the man who had picked up their mother’s body from hospice had been accused of mishandling human remains, they turned to the urn sitting on the table in their mother’s living room.</p><p>They opened it and began to question everything.</p><p>“Where is my mama?” Franquella Campbell, 40, asked over and over.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div healthy for most of her life, say her daughters. She was a hard worker who hated calling off from her job as a supervisor at an Amazon warehouse, where her daughters said she was well-liked and popular among co-workers.</p><p>So it was a shock when she was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare and aggressive cancer that forms in the bile duct.</p><p>Shannon first sought medical care after experiencing frequent stomach pains and losing her sense of taste. Doctors prescribed antibiotics, but they didn’t help, and she was sent home several times from her local clinic. When the pain became unbearable, she went to the hospital, where she was diagnosed with cancer on July 27, 2025.</p><p>“That's when everything started going downhill,” Franquella Campbell said.</p><p>The cancer was advanced, and Shannon needed chemotherapy, but treatment was taking too long to start. She eventually went to another hospital, where doctors were able to begin chemotherapy sooner.</p><p>Then came problems with her disability insurance. Shannon was on short-term disability. When it ran out, her insurance coverage was cut off because she had not yet returned to work. Her family made frequent calls to the insurance company before she was approved for long-term disability.</p><p>But by then, the cancer had spread to other parts of her body, and Shannon would not recover.</p><p>“I just feel like they set my mama up for failure,” Franquella Campbell said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: After lobbyist who's under 65 got tax breaks for seniors, Cook County made him pay up. Then, it renewed them.
entries.summary: <p>Armando W. Saleh, a former Cook County employee turned lobbyist, got more than $20,000 in property tax breaks meant for low-income senior citizens — even though voting records and other government documents say he’s 56 years old.</p><p>How? Saleh submitted a passport to the Cook County assessor’s office that showed him as being 15 years older, according to a Chicago Sun-Times investigation of the government office. </p><p>The passport, issued in March 2021, was among many documents used by Saleh, a former chief of staff to a Cook County commissioner, to secure 69 tax breaks that saved him a total of more than $80,000 under Assessor Fritz Kaegi and two predecessors in that elected position going back to 1998.</p><p>It’s unclear why the three assessors kept approving tax breaks on Saleh’s two homes despite a state law that limits those exemptions to just one, an owner-occupied home.</p><p>Saleh is now the latest of more than a dozen homeowners who have lost their tax breaks following Sun-Times investigations of the county office. The others include former Ald. Walter Burnett, Mayor Brandon Johnson’s former budget director Annette Guzman and the estate of a dead mobster — who kept getting tax breaks in his name even years after he died.</p><p>Property owners must sign applications swearing that they were eligible to get the tax breaks and acknowledging that they could be charged with perjury if they filed a false claim.</p><p>But that's been an empty threat under Kaegi, a lame duck who lost his latest reelection bid. </p><p>“The assessor’s office has not referred any erroneous exemption cases to the state’s attorney’s office for prosecution” since Kaegi took office in 2018, according to Christina Lynch, his office's legal director.</p><p>But now Kaegi’s office says it's weighing whether to ask Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke to investigate Saleh’s tax breaks. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c00000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cook County Assessor Fritz Kaegi. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>It’s hard for county assessors in Illinois, particularly in the Chicago area, to catch people who illegally collect residential property tax breaks. Kaegi’s office relies on whistleblowers to flag relatives, friends and neighbors who might have gotten tax breaks they weren't entitled to, according to a recent report from the Cook County inspector general’s office.</p><h3>Kaegi’s baffling decision</h3><p>The Sun-Times unearthed Saleh’s illegal exemptions nearly two years ago by examining the assessor’s database, looking for red flags. That showed he was taking tax breaks on two homes — including senior exemptions, for which you have to be at least 65 years old to qualify. Saleh and his wife weren't old enough to qualify. They still aren't.</p><p>In 2024, Kaegi ordered Saleh to repay $101,807 to cover 34 tax breaks, penalties and interest he got on his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/gage-park" >Gage Park</a> two-flat and another in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lawndale" >Lawndale</a> over the past seven years. That's all that Kaegi could claw back under state law.</p><p>Saleh, who's now a registered lobbyist for PepsiCo, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/01/17/senior-freeze-property-tax-exemption-fritz-kaegi-armando-saleh-cook-county-assessor-jill-fitzgerald" >repaid</a> the money without putting up a fight.</p><p>But then in 2025, Kaegi’s staff made a baffling decision. It went ahead and renewed Saleh’s tax breaks on both buildings. That cut his property taxes by a total of $2,392 last year, money the office now says he will have to reimburse the county treasury. </p><p>“We also have a photocopy of a U.S. passport on file for Armando Saleh, turned in with an exemption application, that shows he has a birth year of 1955,” Kaegi spokesman Christian Belanger says. "That would make him eligible for the senior exemption. If you have reliable information from voter registration records showing that he isn’t that age, please pass it along to us.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4d0000" name="image-4d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/89ce26e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5b%2F30%2Fa76a7cec4272ab6d74364880cf0a%2Fpassport-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6e27621/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5b%2F30%2Fa76a7cec4272ab6d74364880cf0a%2Fpassport-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c46b831/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5b%2F30%2Fa76a7cec4272ab6d74364880cf0a%2Fpassport-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A copy of Armando W. Saleh's passport facing page, which was submitted to Cook County Assessor Fritz Kaegi's office to obtain a senior tax exemption. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c46b831/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5b%2F30%2Fa76a7cec4272ab6d74364880cf0a%2Fpassport-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ae0fb4a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5b%2F30%2Fa76a7cec4272ab6d74364880cf0a%2Fpassport-1.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c46b831/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5b%2F30%2Fa76a7cec4272ab6d74364880cf0a%2Fpassport-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A copy of Armando W. Saleh’s passport facing page, which was submitted to Cook County Assessor Fritz Kaegi’s office to obtain a senior tax exemption. Redactions made by the assessor’s office.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided.</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But, according to voting records from the city of Chicago and other government records, Saleh was born in August 1970, which makes him 56 years old. And his wife Maria Manzano Saleh is 55. They jointly own both homes that have gotten the tax breaks they had to repay. No one else is listed on the deeds for those properties or the mortgages.</p><p>Saleh didn’t return messages seeking comment about the passport that Kaegi’s staff relied on to award him senior tax cuts, including the lucrative assessment freeze for seniors with household incomes below $65,000.</p><p>“On behalf of Mr. Saleh, we have no comment on your requests,” says his lawyer Ricardo Meza, a former state of Illinois executive inspector general.</p><h3>More erroneous tax breaks</h3><p>Saleh is among more than 9,000 Cook County homeowners Kaegi says have had to repay a total of $59 million in erroneous tax breaks they received. In most cases, they had to pay penalties and interest.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-f10000" name="html-embed-module-f10000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/30082402"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30082402/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Last year, Kaegi’s office approved a variety of tax breaks to 63% of Cook County’s 1,586,788 residential property owners, county records show, shifting $1.58 billion in taxes onto other property owners, including residential and commercial landowners.</p><p>With so many tax breaks granted each year, it’s difficult for Kaegi’s staff to ensure that all of those taxpayers are entitled to those exemptions, especially those based on income, because they have no authority to review income-tax returns.</p><p>“It’s always going to be a constant cat-and-mouse game with people who try to game the system," says Patrick Hynes, the Lyons Township assessor who is aiming to become Cook County’s next assessor following the Nov. 3 election.<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/cook-county-assessor-illinois-primary-results" > Hynes defeated Kaegi </a>in the Democratic primary election last spring. No Republican is seeking to run the office, though Libertarian candidate Nico Tsatsoulis is on the ballot.</p><p>Still, Hynes says, "We have to do a better job of identifying them. I’m the bureaucratic administrator to administer these [tax break] laws that were handed down by” Illinois legislators.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-150000" name="image-150000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0bc8213/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7329x4113+0+387/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F17%2F24%2F5a565e0c4b7facf7633afc3c01a6%2Fcookassessor-260318-01.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7788a76/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7329x4113+0+387/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F17%2F24%2F5a565e0c4b7facf7633afc3c01a6%2Fcookassessor-260318-01.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/79b35a7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7329x4113+0+387/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F17%2F24%2F5a565e0c4b7facf7633afc3c01a6%2Fcookassessor-260318-01.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Lyons Township Assessor Pat Hynes, who will be the next Cook County assessor.
