They paid $144,000, largely financed with a mortgage.</p><p>A year later, they got their first property tax break, the basic homeowner exemption given to anyone who owns and occupies a home. It cut their property tax bill by $403.</p><p>After Saleh landed a job in 1998 as an assistant to then-Cook County Commissioner Joseph Mario Moreno — later promoted to be his chief of staff — he began to get two additional tax breaks from then-Assessor James Houlihan.</p><p>Besides the homeowner exemption, the young couple, who were raising two small children, started collecting the senior citizen exemption along with the low-income senior assessment freeze. Those three tax breaks saved them $661 in taxes, which, like all tax breaks, was money that was shifted to other taxpayers.</p><p>Kaegi’s office says it can't find any records to show how the Salehs qualified for those senior tax breaks, which they kept receiving over the next several years under three assessors: Houlihan, Joseph Berrios and Kaegi.</p><p>Altogether, county records show, the Salehs got 40 senior tax breaks on their Troy two-flat between 1998 and 2023, cutting their real estate taxes by $22,023 — $7,413 from the senior exemption and $14,610 from the low-income senior assessment freeze given to people 65 or older with a household income under $65,000.</p><p>In a brief interview in October 2024, Saleh defended getting the senior tax breaks on his two-flat, saying, “Yeah, but my parents live there.”</p><p>Armando and Maria Saleh are the only people listed on the deed and the mortgage, but a man identified as Ahmad Saleh submitted an application for the senior tax breaks on that property on March 11, 2024, according to Kaegi’s records.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Those applications list four different birthdates for Ahmad Saleh. The first one says he was born in 1925. The next two say he was born in 1945. The fourth says he was born in 1941. The fifth says 1945. And the most recent one says he was born in 1956.</p><p>Chicago election records show Ahmad Saleh, a naturalized citizen born in what used to be Palestine in 1925, was registered to vote from Armando Saleh’s Gage Park house starting in 1996 until his voter registration was canceled in 2012 — the year he allegedly started applying for the senior tax breaks.</p><h3>Another property, more tax breaks</h3><p>Armando Saleh got a job as a community relations officer for the Chicago Transit Authority in 2001, when he and his wife bought another two-flat, on the 2500 block of West Flournoy Street in Lawndale. They paid $150,000 for the building, financing it with a mortgage for $256,800, county records show.</p><p>As with their home on Troy, Armando Saleh and his wife are the only people listed on the deed and the mortgage.</p><p>Nine years later, they started taking homeowner and senior exemptions on the Flournoy building at the same time they also were getting those tax breaks on the Troy home, despite the Illinois law that allow people to collect residential tax breaks on only one property.</p><p>Altogether, Cook County records show, the Salehs got more than $58,000 in tax breaks on the Flournoy property between 2014 and 2023.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f90000" Their relationship isn’t clear.</p><p>Five more applications were submitted under the name of Melba Saleh between 2014 and 2019, though the applications have different birthdates. Three say she was born in 1943, and the others say 1942, according to the assessor’s records.</p><p>Then, in 2022, Kaegi received an application for tax breaks from Armando Saleh, who included a copy of a U.S. passport stating that he was born in Puerto Rico in 1955, which would qualify him for senior tax breaks dating to 2021.</p><p>City voting records, though, show he was born in Puerto Rico in 1970, meaning he’s too young to get senior tax breaks.</p><p>Based on Saleh’s passport, Kaegi kept granting the homeowner and senior exemptions along with the senior freeze. This saved Saleh $26,007 in taxes on the Flournoy property, where he said he was living, though he was registered to vote at his home on Troy.</p><p>After the Sun-Times reported on Saleh’s property tax breaks in November 2024, Kaegi ordered him to repay all of the senior tax breaks he'd gotten on both homes since 2017, along with homeowner exemptions he got on the Flournoy property.</p><p>Five days after the Sun-Times story, Saleh paid the county $86,948, including penalties and interest, for the tax breaks he took on the Flournoy property, along with $14,960 for the senior tax breaks he got on his Troy property.</p><h3>Income-tax problems</h3><p>While Saleh received all of those erroneous exceptions to reduce his property taxes, he also was facing income-tax problems with the Internal Revenue Service and the Illinois Department of Revenue, according to liens filed with the Cook County clerk.</p><p>The IRS filed a lien against Saleh in 2007 to collect $103,397 in income taxes it said he owed from 2001 and 2003. The IRS released that lien in 2013.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Revenue filed a lien against Saleh in 2010, seeking to collect $8,740 in income taxes from 2001. It’s unclear whether Saleh paid those taxes. The lien has never been released.</p><p>The IRS filed another lien against Saleh in 2019, saying he owed $35,886 in income taxes from 2014, 2015 and 2016. That lien hasn’t been released.</p><p>Nearly a year after Saleh repaid the erroneous tax breaks on both two-flats, the county sent him new tax bills last fall, granting him a homeowner and senior exemption on each two-flat.</p><p>That snafu by Kaegi’s office lowered the taxes Saleh paid last fall, saving him $1,196.64 on his Gage Park two-flat and $1,195.76 on the Lawndale two-flat. Kaegi's office says Saleh will have to repay those tax breaks.</p><p>Saleh isn’t receiving any exemptions on his two property tax bills that are due Oct. 1.</p><p>Now that he has lost all of his exemptions, the real estate tax bills on his two properties have soared since the Sun-Times investigation two years ago. This year, Saleh owes $5,005.22 in taxes on his Gage Park two-flat, up from $1,652.05 two years ago. entries.title: Review: BTS’ Arirang World Tour lands in Chicago as the K-pop boy band evolves into version 2.0
entries.summary: <p>The seven-year itch has finally been scratched.</p><p>BTS returned to Chicago Thursday night for the first time since 2019, reigniting the immense love of their fan Army. Since kicking off in April, the Arirang World Tour has become the pop culture event of the year, staging the boy band’s long overdue reunion after all seven members completed required military service in Korea.</p><p>As the juggernaut made its way to Soldier Field for some of the final dates of the North American run (including Friday’s finale), the 60,000-plus people that sold out the stadium came ready to celebrate what even Governor Pritzker proclaimed as “BTS Day.”</p><p>All week, local news helicopters captured fans lining up as early as 3 a.m. to have a chance at hot-ticket merch items at pop-up stations around the stadium. By the time Thursday came around, most were tagged as “sold out.” Fans had their arms full with the bounty, along with signs (many in Korean), international flags, BTS dolls and the homemade keychains, friendship bracelets and sticker packets they handed out like Halloween candy. If you didn’t have a piece of the DIY paraphernalia or one of the $69 light sticks, you were in a very clear minority.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of HYBE/BIGHIT MUSIC</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Inside the stadium, between relaxing bits of Korean folk music, a very dramatic narrator on giant video screens explained how to use the light wands, as if they were getting the Army ready for battle. It added to an apocalyptic, sci-fi vibe anchored by the massive 360-degree stage that looked like a docked spaceship.</p><p>The set design was actually a heritage marker, meant to evoke the jeongja-style pavilions of Seoul, with jutting runways reminiscent of the four trigrams on the South Korean flag. The design also allowed each member equal time with different sections of the stadium, ramping up the scream-o-meter with every move. But the monstrosity was nothing more than a heap of steel without the boy band animating the space.</p><p>Chants of “BTS! BTS!” filled the stadium around the official start time of 8 p.m. as fans grew impatient. As things finally got underway 20 minutes later, the deafening screams and audible “oh my Gods” heard throughout the bowl brought Beatlemania to mind. A runner raced out of the Bears tunnel carrying a torch trailing plumes of red smoke as if Olympians were descending.</p><p>The first five minutes of the night packed in a dizzying amount of overstimulation: Flags waved and fireworks exploded as a 100-person procession of dancers ushered the seven-man group to the stage.</p><p>Over the next two hours, the Bangtan Boys lived up to the hype: RM, Jin, SUGA, j-hope, Jimin, V and Jung Kook whipped through a spell-binding amount of material. The night started off with the hip-hop flavors of “Hooligan” and “Aliens” and moved through fan favorites, including the straightforward pop song “Normal,”the slowed down ballad “Like Animals” and the dance/EDM explosion of “FYA” into “Fire,” during which the stadium seemed to shake as fans jumped to the music.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of HYBE/BIGHIT MUSIC</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Each band member leaned into his strength — Jimin with his falsetto and RM, SUGA, and J-Hope as rhyme slayers — and amplified their talents for the betterment of the group. When the members physically came together in the center of the stage for riveting moments of choreography, the chemistry felt like no time had passed.</p><p>But BTS was clearly focused on the present and future of the group.</p><p>The evening focused largely on BTS’ March release, “Arirang,” which felt like a purposeful introduction to the group’s refined version “2.0” alluded to on the album. By now, the boy band are now all men, and the K-pop they helped to define as vanguards of the genre seems to be something they want to rewrite.</p><p>“Arirang” has a heavier street style with more Western R&B and hip-hop flair and English-language lyrics, and the band worked with producers like Diplo, Ryan Tedder and JPEGMafia to birth this metamorphosis. The Army loved it — a song like “FYA” was better received than even past pop hits like “Dynamite” and “Butter.”</p><p>BTS also recently declined to submit any new music for the 2027 Recording Academy Awards, refusing to be lumped into the new Best Asian Pop Music category. All of it points to a push-and-pull evolution of BTS’ future, something they grapple with in a song like “Aliens” and in their recent Netflix documentary, “The Return,” about furthering their global status while recognizing their roots.</p><p>Human moments like these stood out during the evening: After the night’s scripted parts wound down, the band performed two “surprise songs,” “Tomorrow” and “Hip-Hop Phile,” followed by all members of BTS casually sitting down on a rotating platform to give end-of-night speeches.</p><p>Using a translator, Jung Kook fondly remembered the last time BTS played Chicago in the rain and shouted out the fans who planned to come back for day two, of which there were many, judging by the applause. SUGA thought back to his solo D-Day tour he brought to the city in 2023, while RM remembered his own solo trip to the Art Institute in 2018 which “opened a big interest for me into the art world” he said, tying it back to his exhibition opening at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art this fall.</p><p>But it was J-Hope talking about his groundbreaking Lollapalooza solo debut in 2022 that drove the feelings home for the local crowd. “Chicago is one of the places that made me who I am as an artist,” he said. “I feel like Chicago has its own folder in my head … and tonight on the Arirang Tour with you guys I’m going to save this one in there too. Thanks for all the memories, you guys mean so much to us.”</p><p><i>BTS returns to Soldier Field on Friday.</i></p><p></p><h3>BTS Arirang World Tour set list</h3><p>Hooligan<br>Aliens<br>Run BTS<br>They Don’t Know ’Bout Us<br>Like Animals<br>Fake Love<br>Swim<br>Merry Go Round<br>2.0<br>Normal<br>Not Today<br>Mic Drop<br>FYA<br>Fire<br>Body To Body<br>Idol<br>Come Over<br>Butter<br>Dynamite<br>Tomorrow<br>Hip Hop Phile<br>Please<br>Into The Sun</p>

entries.title: Trump administration appeals latest ruling blocking his mail voting order from taking effect
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON — The Trump administration is appealing a judge’s ruling that blocked <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/donald-trump-mail-voting-elections-47cc334b1fb7742244a9c4f176b355cd" target="_blank" >limitations on mail voting</a> before the midterm elections, the latest twist in a court fight unfolding days before the first states begin sending out mail ballots for the pivotal November elections.</p><p>The notice of appeal filed Friday comes after a federal judge in Boston handed down a <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-voting-mail-ballots-democrats-lawsuits-15cf1ec7dcdb8211bf6b624b75a7f4ab" target="_blank" >new decision blocking implementation</a> of an executive order from <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/donald-trump" target="_blank" >President Donald Trump</a> for the next two weeks.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-mail-voting-supreme-court-157afc3c195ce0a62c522da5ce904b04" target="_blank" >Supreme Court</a> previously allowed the plan to move ahead on procedural grounds, but hasn’t decided whether it’s legal. The U.S. 1st Circuit Court of Appeals will next consider the case, though it could soon be back before the nation's highest court.</p><p>Under Trump’s executive order, the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/postal-service-midterms-trump-mail-voting-b4b9ef095b4d6bceab18adbb34814640" target="_blank" >U.S. Postal Service</a> could refuse to deliver ballots from states that do not submit lists of eligible voters and follow a uniform envelope style. The White House calls the plan a set of “commonsense measures” aimed at protecting ballot security, and calls the order blocking it “unreasoned and unlawful.”</p><p>The plaintiffs didn't have immediate comment on the appeal.</p><p>U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani found that states don't have the time or money to design and produce new ballots, update their systems and train officials to upload voter data to the Postal Service in the short time before the midterm elections.</p><p>The first mail ballots of the general election to determine control of Congress are scheduled to be sent out Sept. 4.</p><p>Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker on Friday called out the Trump administration for attempting to push through restrictive rules on mail-in voting ahead of the November election. At a press conference in downstate Carbondale, Pritzker said Trump is trying to stop people from voting because "he knows he and his party are going to lose in November."</p><p>"For many people, voting by mail is the best option. For many, it's the only option. And so, at least in Illinois, we're going to protect that," Pritzker said. "It's up to the states to run elections, not up to Donald Trump or the federal government."</p><p>The Thursday ruling came after Democrats and voting rights groups <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-voting-mail-ballots-midterms-executive-order-7ed54dda90705ff169d0a022f6a1dde9" target="_blank" >filed a fresh round of lawsuits</a> to comply with the recent Supreme Court decision. They note that the Constitution grants states and, in some cases, Congress the power to make election rules — not the president or Postal Service.</p><p>Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, who represented Illinois as one of 25 states seeking to block implementation of Trump's order, praised Talwani's ruling. </p><p>“The U.S. Constitution is clear: States have the power to administer elections, not the federal executive branch, and I will continue to fight against this blatantly unconstitutional rule that would only create disorder and undermine confidence in our upcoming general election,” Raoul said. “In granting this TRO, the court has acknowledged that states do not have the time to completely overhaul their mail-in ballot procedures to comply with a Postal Service rule we argue is not even constitutional in the first place. This attempt by the Trump administration to interfere with our elections process is part of the administration’s efforts to interrupt our citizens’ access to voting.”</p><p>The whipsawing legal battle could have major ramifications for the midterms. Nearly one-third of Americans <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/election-2024-voting-mail-ballots-drop-boxes-a92707d4805ea2701a8d795e39f83241" target="_blank" >vote by mail</a> and election officials contend there isn’t enough time to revise their systems to comply with the new Postal Service directives.</p><p>The president has <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/f0a5b003db26dbb19778bcdcb45f9a3f" target="_blank" >long targeted mail voting</a>, which he falsely blames for his 2020 election loss even though <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/donald-trump-vote-by-mail-bd52fd205f4484237d5b77d2e7319350" target="_blank" >he himself uses it</a> to cast his ballot. A report by the Brookings Institution published in 2025 found that mail voting fraud occurred in only about four cases out of every 10 million mail ballots cast.</p><p>Trump's executive order was challenged in court shortly after being issued in March. Talwani, nominated to the bench by President Barack Obama, agreed to block it for the midterm elections. But the Supreme Court found earlier this week that she had acted too soon. The Post Office plan has <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/postal-service-midterms-trump-mail-voting-b4b9ef095b4d6bceab18adbb34814640" target="_blank" >since been finalized</a>.</p><p><i>Contributing: WBEZ Springfield reporter Isabela Nieto</i></p>
entries.author: Lindsay Whitehurst | Associated Press

entries.title: At Chicago State University, football is a whole new ballgame
entries.summary: <p>Linebacker Mark Pullman followed a tight end into the flat, slipped in front of him for an interception and took it back for a house call.</p><p>All the way across the left-field foul line.</p><p>Wait, what?</p><p>This was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >football practice at Chicago State University</a> less than 48 hours before the first game in school history, which is at noon Saturday against Division II Roosevelt at SeatGeek Stadium in Bridgeview. Chicago State — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2025/04/09/chicago-state-cougars-football-bobby-rome-bears-ben-johnson-nfl" target="_blank" >debuting as an independent in the Division I FCS ranks</a> — will be the home team.</p><p>Why Bridgeview? Because Chicago State doesn’t have a stadium.</p><p>Why the left-field foul line? Because the Cougars don’t have a football practice facility.</p><p>Instead, they’re putting in daily work on the school’s baseball field. Did I mention Chicago State doesn’t have a baseball team?</p><p>After Pullman’s practice pick, his defensive teammates joined him for a celebration in the end zone, which is to say a strip of turf between the foul line and a chain-link fence. Snatching up the ball and spiking it to players’ delight was assistant head coach and defensive line coach Kentwan Balmer, one man on the field whose name resonates in football circles. Balmer was a first-round NFL draft pick in 2008 and played for the 49ers and Seahawks.</p><p>While the offense and defense went at it in the outfield, specialists worked where they could. Punters Donovan Blair and Jordan Zimmerman — who double as the team’s placekickers — booted balls from deep in the hole at shortstop toward a teammate waiting near where home plate would be if bases were in the dirt. Practice culminated with the offense in the two-minute drill, leading to a Blair field-goal try on the final play that either split the proverbial uprights or drifted a bit wide right. Had there been goal posts anywhere in sight — no, the Cougars don’t have those, either — I’d have been able to tell you.</p><p>This, folks, is what’s known as starting at the very bottom.</p><p>“Everyone has to start from somewhere, you know what I mean?” head coach Bobby Rome said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2025/04/09/chicago-state-cougars-football-bobby-rome-bears-ben-johnson-nfl" target="_blank" >I wrote about Rome</a> after interviewing him on his first official day on the job, in April of last year. He had no clue where the Cougars would practice or play games. He had no staff and hadn’t begun looking for players. At best, he was in for a more challenging task than the average coach could even imagine.</p><p>A football team out of thin air at Chicago State? I had to see it with my own eyes just to wrap my brain around it. Most of the school’s other sports teams struggle mightily just to keep their heads above water in the Northeast Conference, which the football team will join in 2027. The Cougars’ men’s and women’s basketball teams were a combined 16-48 last season. The women’s volleyball team was 1-25. The men’s and women’s soccer teams are a combined 0-7 this season. You get the picture.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Bobby Rome addresses his team <a href="https://x.com/chicagostatefb?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@chicagostatefb</a>. The Cougars play Saturday for the first time ever. My column soon. <a href="https://t.co/BgNHpXUwb9">pic.twitter.com/BgNHpXUwb9</a></p>— Steve Greenberg (@SLGreenberg) <a href="https://x.com/SLGreenberg/status/2093441440688849121?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 28, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Chicago State’s enrollment of approximately 2,500 is well below the average in the Northeast — and across the FCS — but the good news is 92 students at the predominantly Black public school in Roseland on the Far South Side spend much of their time wearing shoulder pads and helmets. Somehow, Rome and his cast of eager assistant coaches found them all.</p><p>I asked Rome, 40, how many eight-hour nights of sleep he has had over the past 17 months.</p><p>“None,” he said. “Not even gonna lie to you.”</p><p>Rome, who played with Balmer — not to mention Bears coach Ben Johnson — at North Carolina, is no average coach. His first coaching job was in Vladivostok, Russia, the eastern terminus of the Trans-Siberian Railway, close to the borders of China and North Korea. Back stateside, he served as head coach at three HBCUs. At the first, he inherited a 44-game losing streak. At the next, things shut down almost immediately due to the COVID-19 pandemic. And at the one after that, the football program was fresh off a 62-year hiatus.</p><p>“I’m battle-tested, man,” he said. “I’ve been doing this for a while.”</p><p>How much resolve can one man have?</p><p>I tip my helmet to Rome for having whatever it is inside him that leads him to these opportunities and urges him to keep saying yes. Most coaches wouldn’t dare.</p><p>A lot of players would turn the other way, too, rather than commit to play on a team that might have a lot of growing to do before it can realistically think about winning games at a level one notch below the big-bopper FBS.</p><p>“We’re building it brick by brick,” said wide receiver Arshawn Powell, who redshirted at Southern Illinois last season after scoring 13 touchdowns as a senior at Evergreen Park. “It’s not about us. It’s for Chicago.”</p><p>The roster includes 20 players from Chicago and five others from Illinois, part of a mash-up of hopefuls who are new to college football or have experienced it for various lengths of time — some seeing game action, others not — elsewhere.</p><p>One of them is wide receiver Kayman Coleman, who’s a handful of college stops, two broken collarbones and one job as a security guard removed from his standout days at Von Steuben. But he’s back in the game and fired up about it.</p><p>“It’s a great opportunity,” Coleman said. “You can’t beat being at home with the people you love, who’ve been supporting you your whole life, and getting to build something from the ground up. It’s like a dream come true.”</p><p>What’s it going to look like on game days?</p><p>“Like a bunch of competitive young men who understand we’re fighting for something bigger than us,” Rome said.</p><p>Here's to ’em, then. Onward and upward.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2025/04/09/chicago-state-cougars-football-bobby-rome-bears-ben-johnson-nfl" target="_blank" >Chicago State’s first football coach, Bobby Rome II, took a path to the city that you won’t believe</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Steve Greenberg

entries.title: King's upset of St. Laurence proved the Jaguars on the rise
entries.summary: <p>Add another name to the list of Public League football powers on the South Side.</p><p>Morgan Park, Simeon and Kenwood have been getting most of the attention in recent years. But they're no longer alone in boosting the city's reputation in the larger Illinois prep football community.</p><p>King was a longtime Public League force under coach Lonnie Williams before having a bit of a down period after his retirement. Now, fifth-year coach Abdullah Asad and some Division I prospects have the Jaguars back on the radar.</p><p>King's Week 1 result — a 15-14 comeback win at Catholic League power St. Laurence — put an exclamation point on the program's recent rise.</p><p>The Jaguars trailed 14-3 after three quarters against the Vikings, who were a Class 6A semifinalist last season and have reached the quarterfinals or beyond six times since 2015.</p><p>"It meant a lot, man," said junior running back Jamar Lewis, a four-star prospect with five Power Four offers. "It's like we [are] making a statement in the city and [to] the [Catholic League], like we can play with anybody."</p><p>Cornelius Moore, a 6-5, 340-pound senior offensive tackle committed to Florida Atlantic, seconded that.</p><p>"It meant a lot to us, especially the development part we had [gone] through since we [weren't] really doing that well," he said. "And now we have developed into a greater team and we wore them out."</p><p>"Getting our kids to where we want to get them to, you've got to play the Catholic schools," Asad said. And then we just talk about the state playoffs. You've got to be able to play the quality opponents as you go through, so that was big for our schedule in the preseason."</p><p>The Jaguars' motto for the season is "fast, physical, disciplined." That last one was a big point of emphasis over the offseason.</p><p>"The last couple seasons when we went to the state playoffs, it was literally like penalties were killing us," Asad said. "We didn't have a lot of penalties [against St. Laurence], so that discipline piece was really, really big for us."</p><p>Asad has led the Jaguars to four straight winning seasons and three IHSA playoff berths, and seen them return to the top-tier Red division last season. But his plan for the program's long-term sustainability goes beyond wins and losses.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8f0000" name="image-8f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/464304b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4184x2348+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2F09%2Fe9d62a334c0f8caa4947821a691f%2Fmc-cst-082726-005.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ec15646/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4184x2348+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2F09%2Fe9d62a334c0f8caa4947821a691f%2Fmc-cst-082726-005.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/db38c3d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4184x2348+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2F09%2Fe9d62a334c0f8caa4947821a691f%2Fmc-cst-082726-005.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="King’s Herman Yancey (red jersey) carries the ball during a drill at practice on Wednesday. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/db38c3d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4184x2348+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2F09%2Fe9d62a334c0f8caa4947821a691f%2Fmc-cst-082726-005.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2b08674/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4184x2348+0+0/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2F09%2Fe9d62a334c0f8caa4947821a691f%2Fmc-cst-082726-005.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/db38c3d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4184x2348+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2F09%2Fe9d62a334c0f8caa4947821a691f%2Fmc-cst-082726-005.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>King’s Herman Yancey (red jersey) carries the ball during a drill at practice on Wednesday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kirsten Stickney/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The program's growth has mirrored that of the school. King's official enrollment is 856, but Asad said the actual number is closer to 1,000 — about double what it was when he arrived.</p><p>Also showing up more these days are college recruiters. Besides Lewis and Moore, senior safety Emmanuel James and senior lineman Damare Griffin have Division I offers.</p><p>The Jaguars split their practice time between two locations. One is Mandrake Park, which is about seven blocks away, has a turf football field and formerly hosted Phillips' home games. The other is a grass field a half-block north of the campus and tucked behind now-closed Price Elementary School.</p><p>Asad said the short-term goal is to upgrade the latter to a full-time practice field lined for football and including goalposts. The longer-term dream is to possibly expand the footprint and build a stadium that could host football games and track meets, among other events.</p><p>"You've got to come in and put your own spin on the whole program," Asad said. "I played college football [at Concordia-St. Paul], I came from Morgan Park High School. So establishing culture within the building was something that was big. ...</p><p>"We started out with about 21 kids when I took over and this year we have about 110 kids inside the program. So it's been fun."</p>

entries.title: Illinois prosecutors fed ICE information about immigrants, leading to arrests and deportations
entries.summary: <p>Rolando Perez Samayoa had come to the United States in 2023 seeking safety. Fleeing violence in Mexico, he’d first planned to make a life in Alabama but had been told that Illinois would protect immigrants like him. </p><p>“There’s some kind of law there,” he said. “It’s supposed to be a sanctuary.”</p><p>He was referring to the state’s 2017 TRUST Act, which was meant to keep local law enforcement out of federal deportation efforts. Samayoa made his way to southern Illinois and found work cleaning a factory. After a DUI arrest in Marion County last October, Samayoa said, he attended his hearings — a fact confirmed by court records.</p><p>In late January, John Christeson, an assistant state’s attorney in the office prosecuting the case, emailed an agent with Homeland Security Investigations, a division of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, about Samayoa. The message included his date of birth, an upcoming court date and where he lived: Centralia, Illinois.</p><p>“Ok, we’ll take care of it, thank you,” the federal agent, Sergio Fulgencio, wrote back minutes later. Two days later, he wanted to know more: “Do you have any reports on this guy?”</p><p>Christeson sent him the police report and related tickets. Three weeks later, federal agents apprehended Samayoa outside his home. They hauled off his 17-year-old son, too.</p><p>The exchange is among dozens of emails that reveal a pattern of consequential collaboration between county prosecutors and federal immigration agencies across Illinois during the first 15 months of President Donald Trump’s second term.</p><p>State’s attorneys offices in one out of every 6 Illinois counties acted as valuable assets of federal immigration enforcement, sharing sensitive personal data about the people they were prosecuting without criminal warrants, public disclosure or legislative oversight, and with no accounting of how often it happened or who was affected.</p><p>Sometimes, prosecutors volunteered information on their own. Other times, they simply answered when Department of Homeland Security agents came calling. The correspondence crossed party lines and included everyone from paralegals to elected state’s attorneys. The collaboration typically happened without the knowledge of defendants or their attorneys.</p><p>The TRUST Act bars police and other agencies from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/07/25/chicago-federal-judge-dismisses-doj-lawsuit-over-sanctuary-policies-but-gives-feds-another-chance" target="_blank" >helping federal agents deport people</a> absent a federal criminal warrant. But the law doesn’t squarely answer whether prosecutors and their staff are bound by those same restrictions.</p><p>Since Trump took office for the second time, his administration has ramped up immigration enforcement, detention and deportation, and ICE has visibly displayed its enforcement at worksites, front yards and courthouses. In response, states including New York have joined Illinois and more than a dozen others in barring local police and sheriffs from helping with federal immigration enforcement. But the scale of prosecutor collaboration in Illinois — which is one of the largest sanctuary states, and often cited as a national model — raises questions about the limitations of state laws to protect immigrants.</p><p>Injustice Watch filed Freedom of Information Act requests with all 102 Illinois state’s attorney’s offices and drew on records from federal and circuit courts. Together, those internal emails and case files ran more than 5,000 pages. The documents reveal that prosecutors shared much more than just names. Their emails contain photographs. Home addresses. The date and time a defendant was due in court or set to leave jail — the exact window for ICE to make an arrest.</p><p>Eleven offices didn’t respond; some produced records only after they were sued under FOIA. The rest remain in litigation.</p><p>And the written record may be only part of the story. Messages with phrases like “Thank you for taking my call” point to conversations no records requests could follow.</p><p>None of it was inevitable. Dozens of Illinois county prosecutors, faced with the same federal pressure, claimed they had no record of contact with ICE, and at least one made a point of shutting it out — suggesting every act of collaboration was a choice.</p><p>And the choices had consequences: People flagged to ICE were detained and deported, tearing families apart.</p><p>DHS did not answer questions about how its agents work with local officials in Illinois.</p><p>Antonio Gutierrez, who co-founded the advocacy group Organized Communities Against Deportations, was among those who pushed for the TRUST Act. Residents wanted “to trust in local police, in local prosecutors, in the criminal justice system, to be fully separated from immigration and deportation enforcement,” Gutierrez said.</p><p>The records prove that trust was never warranted, Gutierrez said.</p><h3>The ones who were willing — and those who weren’t</h3><p>Twenty minutes after flagging Samayoa, Marion County’s Christeson emailed Fulgencio again.</p><p>“I’ve got another potential,” he wrote, flagging a man with a local warrant who had been arrested on an unrelated charge in Missouri.</p><p>Fulgencio replied that agents were already tracking the man on a civil removal order — a deportation order from an immigration court — and asked whether the county warrant should take priority.</p><p>“Our warrant will not take priority over removal,” Christeson answered.</p><p>Fulgencio wrote back just 34 minutes later: “He’s in ICE Custody awaiting removal.”</p><p>Christeson didn’t respond to questions about his correspondence with Staffers answered ICE’s requests for information and offered specific cases for federal agents to pursue.</p><p>In April 2025, for example, a Customs and Border Protection officer based at O’Hare International Airport asked an assistant prosecutor for records tied to a voter fraud investigation. JB Pritzker speaks to reporters about an increase in political violence at Harold Washington College in the Loop in September 2025.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But the courthouse law was written to stop the agent waiting on the sidewalk, not the prosecutor inside.</p><p>Nearly all the defense attorneys whose clients appear in the records said they had no idea prosecutors were sharing case information with federal immigration agents. They spoke on the condition of anonymity, several citing concern about straining relationships with the prosecutors they face in court, others pointing to cases that are still pending.</p><p>Legal scholars described the collaboration between federal immigration agents and local prosecutors as unprecedented.</p><p>“I cannot recall a single instance in my past practice where an individual within the state’s attorney’s office shared information with ICE,” said University of Kentucky assistant law professor Matthew Boaz.</p><p>Still, he said in an email, “the sentiment of the TRUST Act — separating state/local criminal law enforcement from federal civil immigration enforcement — would seem to include any actor within the criminal legal system.”</p><p>Prosecutors themselves couldn’t agree on whether the TRUST Act applied to them.</p><p>Some said their offices are bound by it. The act covers law enforcement agencies; DuPage County’s Berlin said that includes him and his staff.</p><p>“The State’s Attorney’s Office is charged with enforcement of state, county, and municipal laws,” he said. “Therefore, the law applies to my office.”</p><p>Others said the law doesn’t reach them. Lake County’s Rinehart said his office doesn’t arrest or detain people, so it isn’t a law enforcement agency as defined by the act. Yet Rinehart said his office declines to collaborate with federal immigration enforcement regardless.</p><p>These two offices staked out the clearest positions, landing on opposite sides of the question — and on opposite ends of the spectrum of collaboration. Berlin said his office was bound by the TRUST Act, but it contacted federal immigration officials more than any other. Rinehart said his office wasn’t bound by it, yet shut ICE out entirely. (Neither office tracks its contact with ICE. While police departments and sheriff’s offices must file annual TRUST Act compliance reports, state’s attorneys aren’t required to do so.)</p><p>Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, the state’s chief legal officer, didn’t resolve the question.</p><p>“Applying the TRUST Act in practice requires state and local enforcement to navigate complex interactions in circumstances that are not always clear-cut,” he said in a statement, without answering whether county prosecutors are bound by the law he enforces.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" prosecutors, whether the state should track their contacts with ICE, or whether Illinois has kept its promises to its residents.</p><p>For Samayoa, the question of whom the law binds is beside the point.</p><p>Whatever idea he had about Illinois being a sanctuary ended in February, when ICE agents descended on him in his front yard as he was stepping out to grab a belated birthday dinner. He said eight agents pointed their guns at his teen son, who was trying to reach him as ICE moved in.</p><p>“Everything was going smoothly until his 17 year old son thought he would help his dad out by trying to run over the agents,” Homeland Security’s Fulgencio wrote to Marion County’s Christeson after the incident. “Ended up damaging a vehicle. So now [his son’s] going with him.”</p><p>Samayoa denied that his son tried to run over the agents. DHS defended the way its agents handled the arrest.</p><p>“ICE law enforcement officers are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers,” a spokesperson said in a statement. “Officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training.”</p><p>Samayoa and his son were taken to St. Louis, where he said he felt pressured to agree to leave the country rather than fight his case. He directed his son to do the same. The Department of Homeland Security confirmed both father and son “accepted a voluntary departure.” Within hours, both were on a plane to Texas.</p><p>After one night in an El Paso hotel, Samayoa said, he and his son were escorted across the border into Ciudad Juarez, where he destroyed all immigration paperwork he had with him — vowing to never return to the United States. DHS confirmed both were removed from the United States on Feb. 25.</p><p>Father and son spent time in a shelter before scraping together bus fare to their native state of Chiapas. Back in Illinois, the rest of the family had to raise their own fare south; two months passed before they were all together again.</p><p>Samayoa said he didn’t know that a prosecutor had shared information about him with federal immigration authorities before the raid. </p><p>He said he’d warn the community he left behind in Illinois: Showing up for prosecutors could mean showing up for ICE.</p><p><i>This story was produced by </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Injustice Watch</i></a> <i>in partnership with</i> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wired.com/" target="_blank" ><i>WIRED</i></a><i>. entries.title: Cubs activate Matt Shaw from injured list, option Kevin Alcantara to Triple-A
entries.summary: <p>It took him much longer than he expected, but utility man Matt Shaw returned to the Cubs’ active roster Friday after missing almost two months with a sprained left hand. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> activated him from the injured list and optioned outfielder Kevin Alcantara to Triple-A Iowa.</p><p>Shaw hurt his hand on a normal swing June 28 in Milwaukee. He thinks the injury was a fluke and doesn’t see it becoming a recurring problem. He knows he had never experienced an injury that kept him out for that long.</p><p>“Nothing like this,” Shaw said. “It was one of those things where I assumed it was going to be quicker, and it ended up taking a really long time. It tested my patience, for sure.”</p><p>Shaw went 6-for-19 (.316) in a five-game rehab assignment at Iowa. He said he felt “awesome” Wednesday after playing a day game that followed a night game.</p><p>“The big thing is feeling confident in games,” Shaw said. “I got some good swing speeds. By the fourth or fifth game, I finally started to feel confident where I wasn’t really thinking about it anymore. I just hit. That was the point that I wanted to be in.”</p><p>Shaw wasn’t in the lineup Friday against the Reds, but manager Craig Counsell said there was a good chance he would be Saturday. Counsell likes the options Shaw provides, particularly coming off the bench late in games.</p><p>“Matt does a bunch of things well,” Counsell said. “We haven’t run into a ton of situations where we need it, but it’s the late-game stuff. Matt can run the bases, has hit left-handed pitching well and can play infield and outfield. There’s going to be some days where we run into [that], and he’s valuable when he’s on the bench.”</p><p>Shaw, who was hitting .246 with four home runs, 20 RBI and a .737 OPS at the time of the injury, also gives Counsell another option at second base. Regular second baseman Nico Hoerner is filling in at shortstop in place of the injured Dansby Swanson (strained left oblique).</p><p>“We have options, for sure,” Counsell said. “That’s a lot of what Matt does. Matt can be really valuable because he provides options everywhere.”</p><p>Alcantara was hitting .240 (6-for-25) with one homer in four stints with the Cubs this season, spanning 24 games.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: Mob-tied businessman gets 2 years probation for tax fraud linked to sweepstakes gaming industry
entries.summary: <p>A man with ties to the Chicago Outfit was sentenced to two years probation Friday in a tax fraud case linked to the sweepstakes gaming industry. </p><p>Robert "Bobby" Dominic, 67, had been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2025/02/25/man-mob-ties-dodged-taxes-married-girlfriend-block-testimony" target="_blank" >charged in 2025</a> with a conspiracy to defraud the United States, tax evasion and failure to file tax returns. But he only pleaded guilty Friday to a single charge of filing a false tax return during a hearing before U.S. District Judge Elaine E. Bucklo. The judge's sentence includes credit for the time Dominic already spent on pretrial release.</p><p>His indictment alleged that he concealed income from federal authorities by having <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/6/5/23746999/what-are-sweepstakes-machines" target="_blank" >sweepstakes gaming companies</a> pay him through the "sham" businesses. One of those sweepstakes companies was owned by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/10/11/23913020/businessman-james-t-weiss-gets-5-1-2-years-in-prison-for-bribing-2-state-lawmakers-lying-to-the-fbi" target="_blank" >James Weiss</a>, who was sentenced to prison on bribery charges related to the sweepstakes industry.</p><p>Two sweepstakes companies paid nearly $900,000 to one of Dominic's bogus businesses between October 2014 and January 2020, the indictment alleged. Dominic’s girlfriend, who died in January 2020, was the only person formally associated with the business.</p><p>The following month, a second company was formed, according to the indictment. The feds alleged that Dominic had the sweepstakes companies pay his business more than $500,000 in 2020 and 2021 in order “to conceal and avoid reporting his income to the Internal Revenue Service.” The company's sole shareholder, identified only as “Individual B,” became Dominic’s girlfriend sometime before September 2024</p><p>Dominic did work for the sweepstakes companies, but his bogus businesses didn't, prosecutors previously said. They said he “used nominees to receive income on his behalf” from the sweepstakes companies and directed them to enter into an agreement designed to conceal his income.</p><p>But Dominic only admitted to assisting in or advising the preparation of a "false and fraudulent" tax return for one of the companies in 2021, court records show. The return failed to name him as an owner of the company.</p><p>On Friday, prosecutors said Dominic doesn't owe any money to the IRS.</p><p><i>Clarification: An earlier version of this story incorrectly described Dominic's plea. He has pleaded guilty to assisting in or advising the preparation of a false and fraudulent tax return.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2025/02/25/man-mob-ties-dodged-taxes-married-girlfriend-block-testimony" target="_blank" >Man with mob ties dodged taxes, married girlfriend to block her testimony, feds say</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/10/11/23913020/businessman-james-t-weiss-gets-5-1-2-years-in-prison-for-bribing-2-state-lawmakers-lying-to-the-fbi" target="_blank" >James T. Weiss gets 5.5 years in prison for bribing 2 state lawmakers, lying to FBI</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/6/5/23746999/what-are-sweepstakes-machines" target="_blank" >Sweepstakes machines: the gambling devices at the center of Chicago’s latest corruption trial</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Tony Romo facing three more citations in connection with his arrest
entries.summary: <p>Tony Romo is facing three more citations in connection with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/07/31/cbs-puts-tony-romo-on-leave-after-arrest-on-suspicion-of-operating-vehicle-under-the-influence" >his arrest in July</a> that got him placed on leave from his role as CBS' lead analyst on NFL games.</p><p>Romo was arrested July 23 in Wisconsin on suspicion of operating a vehicle while under the influence.</p><p>The case against the former Dallas Cowboys quarterback was amended Thursday to add citations for possessing open intoxicants in a motor vehicle, unsafe passing on the right and first-offense operating while intoxicated. He already had received a citation for refusal to take a test for intoxication after arrest.</p><p>CBS Sports president David Berson said earlier this month that he does not have a timeline for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/08/11/tony-romo-cbs-sports-nfl" >decision about Romo’s future </a>with the network.</p><p>Romo, 46, has been the lead game analyst for CBS' NFL coverage since 2017 after making four Pro Bowl appearances during a playing career that ran from 2004-16 and was spent entirely with Dallas.</p><p>Analyst JJ Watt will join play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson on CBS Sports' lead NFL team during Romo's absence. Their first game will be on Sept. 13, when the Minnesota Vikings host the Green Bay Packers.</p><p>Romo's arrest followed a traffic stop as he was driving south on Interstate 43. According to the Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office, Romo performed poorly on field sobriety tests before getting arrested, booked and released.</p><p>Citations released by the Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office indicated an open bottle of an alcoholic beverage was found in the passenger's side of Romo's black Jeep during an inventory before it was towed.</p><p>Body camera footage released earlier this week showed Romo telling deputies he had been coming from a golf course and was on his way "to visit grandma and grandpa" when he was stopped. A deputy told Romo he suspected him of being impaired because he had "red glassy eyes" and an "odor of an intoxicating alcoholic beverage."</p><p>"Tony accepts full responsibility for his actions and has taken proactive steps to ensure that this isolated civil matter is properly resolved," a Romo spokesperson said in a statement to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel and TMZ. "We are working with local authorities to bring this matter to a close and we are communicating with CBS about next steps."</p><p>Romo went to high school about 35 miles southwest of Milwaukee in Burlington, Wisconsin.</p><p>Romo remains the Cowboys' franchise leader in career touchdown passes with 248. He held the franchise record for career passing yards (34,183) until Dak Prescott overtook him last season.<br></p>

</b>most intense days of “Operation Midway Blitz,” which began nearly one year ago, on Sept. 8. Hundreds of armed, masked agents from all over the country hit the streets in and around Chicago, detaining thousands as cameras rolled.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-portrait-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">This criminal alien's rap sheet is longer than a CVS receipt. He was found and arrested in Chicago with an active protection order from a prior assault arrest. His prior convictions include driving on a suspended/revoked license, DUI, assault, and domestic battery. <a href="https://t.co/GLUmHqEGLY">pic.twitter.com/GLUmHqEGLY</a></p>— CBP (@CBP) <a href="https://x.com/CBP/status/1987905692863283605?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 10, 2025</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>But a Chicago Sun-Times / WBEZ analysis of<b> </b>data from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shows that the surge of ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers to seize and detain thousands of people they called “criminal illegal aliens” proved less effective in Chicago than the quieter<b> </b>efforts they had taken earlier in the second Trump administration — and since then.</p><p>Nearly month for month, the analysis of detainee data shows, last fall’s campaign to remove the “worst of the worst” was more hype than reality.</p><p>Federal officers had greater success detaining convicted murderers, rapists, other sex offenders and people convicted of serious assault in many months before and after the height of the “blitz” than during it, the analysis shows. And just 15% of the immigrants detained in the Chicago area during the fall campaign had a prior criminal conviction, a steady decline from a high of 50% right after President Donald Trump’s inauguration.</p><p>The high-profile efforts proved particularly<b> </b>effective in at least one area: When a detainee had a prior conviction for a “traffic offense.”</p><p>Federal officers also achieved great success in detaining immigrants with a prior DUI conviction, a crime prioritized by flamboyant <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/12/gregory-bovino-border-patrol-deportation-elcentro-california-blowing-rock-boone-north-carolina-migrants-immigration?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=12122025%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=12122025%20Morning%20Edition+CID_14194dceee40c1980c345381fce1370b&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Gregory%20Bovino%20is%20the%20star%20of%20Trumps%20deportation%20show%20%20we%20traced%20his%20roots&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" ><u>Border Patrol Cmdr.</u><b><u> </u></b><u>Greg Bovino</u></a>, who was 12 when his own father served time for drunkenly crashing his car, killing a 26-year-old woman. The Chicago detainee data didn’t specify whether anyone died or got hurt in each DUI.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-640000" name="html-embed-module-640000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-table" data-src="visualisation/30063762"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30063762/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="table visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>‘</b>It does not make sense’</h3><p>When Trump retook the White House in January 2025, vowing to deport millions of immigrants via aggressive enforcement, he rolled out his campaign mainly in Democratic cities that didn’t vote for him, including Chicago.</p><p>By Sept. 8, and the start of Midway Blitz, his Department of Homeland Security dedicated its surge to a victim of a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/09/08/operation-midway-blitz-katie-abraham-illinois-dhs-kristi-noem-donald-trump" target="_blank" ><u> fatal DUI crash downstate</u></a> caused by an undocumented Guatemalan man. He fled the crash on Jan 19, 2025, that killed Katie Abraham, 20, of Glenview, and Chloe Polzin, 21, of Deerfield, and is currently serving a 30-year prison sentence.</p><p>"This operation will target the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens in Chicago,” DHS said in a news release. “If you come to our country illegally and break our laws, we will hunt you down, arrest you, deport you, and you will never return.”</p><p>But as detentions around Chicago skyrocketed, topping 3,800 over the 68 fall days<b>, </b>roughly 8 of every 10 people held at the ICE processing facility in Broadview or in other Chicago locations had no criminal conviction<b>. </b>Six of the 10<b> </b>had civil immigration violations — like overstaying a visa; the rest have an unspecified criminal charge pending.</p><p>A DHS spokesperson responded to an interview request with a written statement that didn’t address the specific findings and attacked the raw ICE data collected by the nonprofit Deportation Data Project that was the basis for the analysis as “cherry-picked.” The statement also says those stats count crimes just in the U.S. and don’t account for those in other countries.</p><p>“Since Day One, DHS law enforcement has been delivering on President Trump’s promise to the American people to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens including murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members, and terrorists,” it read. “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is whether or not they are illegally in the U.S. — full stop.”</p><div class="Enhancement" The Sun-Times and WBEZ looked at initial detentions logged in the Chicago area and at arrests made in the six-county Chicago metro region between Jan. 20, 2025, and Aug. 5, 2026.</p><p>ICE’s nameless data lists the most serious charge for each immigrant convicted of a crime but provides no details on charges pending when detained. Some highlights:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-989970c1-a306-11f1-b30b-ebd19b581553"><li>The data shows that 11 people with sex assault convictions were detained in October, during the height of the fall 2025 deportation campaign. But federal agents detained 18 immigrants with sexual assault convictions in less time, during the last 11 days of January following Trump's inauguration. They captured 12 more in March.</li></ul><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-989970c2-a306-11f1-b30b-ebd19b581553"><li>During the nine weeks of last fall’s deportation campaign, federal officers booked five convicted killers. Yet they had detained the same number just before in August 2025 and an additional six that May. </li></ul><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-989970c3-a306-11f1-b30b-ebd19b581553"><li>They also detained five convicted sex offenders during those fall weeks — but seven in February 2025, six in July and five in May 2026.</li></ul><p>The situation<b> </b>baffles Esteban Salazar. The suburban building engineer has been victimized by an undocumented immigrant who was charged with pointing a gun at him. Simultaneously, he's horrified that his innocent Mexican-born relatives were grabbed off area streets last fall, detained and then deported.</p><p>Carlos Mavarez Viloria, a Venezuelan migrant, had been arrested several times for theft and possessing crack cocaine before February 2024 when he pulled what Salazar described as a polished black Beretta inside a 7-Eleven Downtown.</p><p>The weapon turned out to be a copycat lighter. But Salazar, a married father of two, braced himself for the real thing. As Mavarez reached into his own pants and headed toward Salazar at the back of the store, threatening to shoot him, Salazar grasped his own licensed handgun.</p><p><b>“</b>So when he pulled a firearm on me, I was already at the back of the store. He was waving it at me. I don't know if he got a glimpse of my firearm, but he ran out,” Salazar says.</p><p>Cook County court records show other charges against Mavarez through May 2026, with mixed outcomes.</p><p>“Why the ‘F’ was he not on the first plane or bus back? My wife's uncle who was here for 20 years. He was held, it's ridiculous,” Salazar says. "It's tough. As a Mexican, as a Latino, I try to understand what our government's doing but it does not make sense."</p><h3>Strategy changes that could explain arrest and detention trends last fall</h3><p>Amid the<b> </b>officers sent to the Chicago area last fall, most from Border Patrol and ICE assignments in a dozen other states, the Trump administration unleashed a bevy of social media posts, extolling arrests of the “worst of the worst.”</p><p>“Operation Midway Blitz is making Illinois SAFE again. DHS law enforcement has made over 1,500 arrests across Illinois including of pedophiles, vicious gang members, and armed robbers,” Homeland Security <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/DHSgov/status/1977881560641638834]]" target="_blank" ><u>posted on X</u></a><b> </b>in mid-October.</p><p>Weeks later, from Border Patrol’s X account: “Another bad guy busted! In Chicago, CBP apprehended this Bulgarian illegal alien with a rap sheet including: domestic battery, aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, rape, failure to register as a sex offender. Happy to have him off the streets!”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Another bad guy busted! Happy to have him off the streets! <a href="https://t.co/9c3SL0I8qV">pic.twitter.com/9c3SL0I8qV</a></p>— CBP (@CBP) <a href="https://x.com/CBP/status/1985806077573664781?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 4, 2025</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>A change in arrest methods in Illinois may help explain the actual low rates of detaining immigrants with serious criminal records. </p><p>Federal officers began 2025 pursuing arrests of undocumented immigrants through 15 government enforcement methods. But between September and November 2025, they logged only four methods. During those months, they reported no arrests under the Criminal Alien Program that tracks when incarcerated immigrants finish their criminal sentences. CAP arrests had accounted for about 10% of arrests between January and September before the Blitz began.</p><p>Then, from Sept. 8 through Nov. 14, the percentage of arrests defined as “collateral” outpaced “targeted” ones — 53% versus 46%. So more people were getting picked up randomly than on purpose. But from Nov. 15 through March 2026, long after the bulk of extra federal officers had left Chicago, targeted arrests eclipsed collateral ones, 72% to 13% (no arrest method was specified for the rest).</p><p>Months before Operation Midway Blitz stormed Chicago, Trump’s new “Border Czar” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/donald-trump/2024/12/09/border-czar-tom-homan-donald-trump-chicago-pritzker-brandon-johnson-immigration" target="_blank" ><u>Tom Homan stood in Portage Park</u></a> in December 2024, vowing to make Chicago ground zero for deportations. A month later, TV's Dr. Phil would ride along with ICE agents in Chicago, questioning detainees on camera.</p><p>January 2025 was a high for detaining immigrants previously convicted of sexual assault especially, and for murder.</p><p>“That was right after the inauguration, continuing into the first couple of weeks in February and then tailing off,” Tsao says. “If there are any arguments for ICE entries.title: Man posted Facebook videos showing 'agonizing' deaths of raccoons being burned alive, knifed, mauled: police
entries.summary: <p>A 54-year-old Auburn Gresham man is accused of posting videos on Facebook showing the 'agonizing' deaths of a raccoons being burned alive, knifed, mauled by a dog and run over by a car, officials said. </p><p>Pierre Scarbrough is charged with six misdemeanor counts of depiction of animal cruelty, and was cited for illegal hunting, no valid hunting license and taking, possessing or selling a wild animal, police said. Scarbrough was arrested Wednesday while at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse for an unrelated hearing for a pending felony drug charge.</p><p>Scarbrough, a convicted felon, was scheduled for a detention hearing on the animal abuse allegations Friday. </p><p>Scarbrough was identified as the person responsible for social media posts from July 19-26, 2026 that depict animal cruelty, according to a statement from Chicago police. </p><p>Acting on a confidential tip, the animal crimes investigation unit with the Illinois Department of Natural Resources (IDNR) conducted a search of Scarbrough's Facebook account after someone spotted a Facebook post of a “raccoon being burned alive,” according to a police report.</p><p>After executing a warrant, investigators found Scarbrough posted multiple videos on Facebook that included “burning a raccoon alive while the raccoon is in severe agonizing pain and suffering; murdering a raccoon with a large knife and showing said raccoon’s dead body with blood around the animal; intentionally running over two raccoons with his vehicle, causing their deaths; recording a severely injured raccoon unable to move underneath a vehicle and admitting to deliberately injuring said raccoon; recording a deceased mouse on the sidewalk and admitting to stomping and jumping on said mouse causing its death and posting a recording of a dog mauling a raccoon and shaking it around inside its mouth causing injury,” according a police report.</p><p>Scarbrough, who is a convicted felon, pleaded guilty in 2014 to aggravated domestic battery, a felony, for which he was sentenced to five years, court records show. </p><p>In a <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/prosecutors-father-girlfriend-beat-11-year-old-girl-after-she-ate-his-ice-cream/" target="_blank" >CBS post that cited Sun-Times wire reporting</a>, it was alleged that Scarbrough and his girlfriend beat his 11-year-old daughter with an electrical cord after she allegedly ate his ice cream. <br></p>

entries.title: With Army in his past — and future — Bears LB Jon Rhattigan fights for roster spot
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Whenever <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> linebacker Jon Rhattigan’s NFL career ends, he owes his country five years of military service.</p><p>The West Point graduate doesn’t know when that day will come — or what it will look like. He's willing to do whatever is asked. He’s 27 and has a body beaten up by six years of the NFL. A geospatial information science major, Rhattigan could end up on the front lines — or not. </p><p>“People look at different movies and think it’s all infantry, but there’s truly so many pieces to that puzzle,” he said recently.</p><p>He keeps up on current events, but tries not to think too far ahead.</p><p>“In the meantime," he said, "it’s really, represent as best as you can."</p><p>When the Bears take the field Saturday night for their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/08/27/bears-titans-podcast-caleb-williams-halas-intrigue" target="_blank" >preseason finale</a> against the Titans, Rhattigan will have one last chance to make an impression on his new bosses. Cuts are due the next day, and the Bears will need to whittle their roster from 90 to 53 players — plus another 16 for the practice squad.</p><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson has been coy about whether he’ll play his starters Saturday after working them hard in Thursday’s joint practice. Even if they play briefly, Saturday’s game will be more about the players at the back end of the roster.</p><p>“We got 90 guys on the roster right now, a lot of which are fighting for their professional lives …” Ben Johnson said Thursday. “And their stories are incredible.”</p><p>None more so than Rhattigan, who graduated from Nequa Valley High School in Naperville before being accepted to West Point. He spent his freshman year on the scout team and didn’t play as a sophomore until a blowout bowl game victory. As a junior, he was a third-stringer. He had six tackles in three years.</p><p>He didn’t start until his senior year, when he made one of the season’s highlight plays, stopping Navy’s Xavier Arline at the goal line in a rivalry victory. He was a semifinalist for the Bednarik Award, given to the best defensive player in college football. The Seahawks signed him as an undrafted free agent. When he eventually stuck on the roster as a practice squad player, his mandatory five years’ service was postponed.</p><p>He spent three seasons in Seattle as a special teams stalwart before going to Carolina in 2024. Former Seahawks coach Pete Carroll plucked him off the Steelers practice squad last year to sign with the Raiders.</p><p>Rhattigan went to the Bears’ May rookie minicamp as a veteran tryout player and was signed the next day. It was a surreal moment for someone who grew up with photos of Brian Urlacher and Lance Briggs on his wall.</p><p>“It’s a 1-in-32 chance — and something early in my career I never saw coming to fruition. …” he said. “ It’s awesome that it’s being lived out.”</p><p>If Rhattigan makes the team, it will be because of his special teams play. At linebacker, he’s behind the Bears’ three starters — and perhaps Jack Sanborn and Ruben Hyppolite, too. It’s unclear what the Bears will do with rookie Keyshaun Elliott, who didn’t start practicing until Wednesday.</p><p>Special teams coordinator Richard Hightower can tell he's an Army grad.</p><p>“Just the way he goes about his business,” Hightower said. “Detail-oriented, serious, loves what he does. And cares deeply for others.”</p><p>Rhattigan knows the difference between football and the military — one is entertainment and the other is life and death. But there are similarities, too.</p><p>“There’s so many parallels — facing adversity, dealing with hardships, having to be disciplined, understanding that there’s hard work in front of you and there’s no way around it … “ he said. “It shapes you mentally to be someone who can deal with adversity. entries.title: Man, 42, killed in ATV crash in Ashburn
entries.summary: <p>A 42-year-old man was killed Friday afternoon when his ATV struck a Nissan Rogue in a collision in Ashburn, Chicago police said.</p><p>The crash took place along the 8400 block of South Pulaski Road at about 2:08 p.m, police said.</p><p>The unidentified man had been taken to Christ Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, according to police.</p><p>The Major Accidents Investigation Unit is investigating.</p>

entries.title: Cubs' key relievers might be regressing to mean at worst time
entries.summary: <p>Some stalwarts in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs’</a> bullpen might be regressing to the mean, and they sure picked a lousy time to do it.</p><p>After starter David Peterson at least gave the Cubs a chance to win, pitching five innings of two-run ball, Trent Thornton all but removed it, allowing five runs in the sixth inning of an eventual 10-8 loss to the Reds at Wrigley Field.</p><p>Thornton hadn’t allowed a run in August, spanning 10 innings in 11 games. But his ERA went from zero to 4.22 with the two-thirds-of-an-inning outing, in which he allowed a two-run homer to light-hitting catcher Jose Trevino and a three-run blast to Tyler Stephenson.</p><p>“He made some bad pitches, and they hit them,” manager Craig Counsell said. “Trent’s been really, really good for a good stretch here, but he made some bad pitches today.”</p><p>Thornton, who didn’t make himself available to talk, wasn’t alone. In his third outing since returning from elbow inflammation, Daniel Palencia turned a one-run ninth-inning deficit into two, allowing a home run to TJ Friedl, who looked very proud of his fourth homer of the season.</p><p>All of this follows closer Jacob Webb’s implosions on the Cubs’ painful 2-4 road trip through Seattle and Phoenix. After not allowing a run in 24 consecutive appearances, Webb allowed five in two, each capped by walk-off homers.</p><p>Before that run of success, he had a 3.90 ERA through 33 outings. He brought it down to 2.21 after that run. Now it’s on the way back up, perhaps an indication of fatigue as he inches closer to matching his career high in innings pitched (66). He’s at 58⅔.</p><p>Counsell said there are no plans to give him a break.</p><p>“Relievers that have good years, that’s what happens — they get to that point,” he said. “We’re going to need Jacob to be good to accomplish our goals. You’re always monitoring workload; it’s a daily thing. I think Jacob’s in a good spot.”</p><p>What about Ryan Zeferjahn? After looking good for the Angels, he has looked anything but for the Cubs since coming over before the trade deadline. In nine games for his new club, Zeferjahn has a 6.75 ERA.</p><p>Left-hander Caleb Thielbar isn’t close to the reliable reliever he was last season, when he had a 2.64 ERA in 67 games. This season, he’s at 5.09 in 48. Perhaps the only reason Colin Rea has been spared is because he hasn’t pitched in a week. Counsell said that has been because of game situations, nothing about Rea’s health.</p><p>Lefty Ryan Rolison, who’s sporting a 2.82 ERA in 47 games, best beware. He might be the next to regress. He had a 7.02 ERA in 31 games last season, though it came with a Rockies club that lost 119 games, two shy of the 2024 White Sox’ major-league record.</p><p>The loss moved the Cubs a half-game closer to the furthest they’ve been from the first-place Brewers all season — eight games. It’s looking more and more like those seven games against the Brewers in 10 days, beginning Monday, will only serve to extend the distance between them.</p><p>Peterson wasn’t great — he allowed six hits and three walks — but as Counsell said, he gave the Cubs a chance, handing a 3-2 lead to the bullpen. He had thrown 88 pitches but said there was no discussion of going out for the sixth inning.</p><p>That honor went to Thornton, who looked nothing like he had, adding to the bullpen’s struggles. Aaron Civale allowed two runs in the seventh, though both were unearned, thanks to third baseman Alex Bregman’s error.</p><p>Even a 13-hit performance — including a two-run homer by Michael Busch and a three-run blast by Pedro Ramirez — couldn’t make up for what the relievers wrought.</p><p>“We gave up 10 today,” Counsell said. “It’s going to be tough winning games giving up 10.”</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true"
