entries.title: Sam Antonacci creating 'pandemonium' on the basepaths, whether White Sox manager Will Venable likes it or not
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — Running straight at an infielder poised to launch a throw inches from his face?</p><p>That’s just <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> grinder Sam Antonacci, who put his provocative base-running style on display yet again in the sixth inning of Wednesday’s game against the Rangers.</p><p>The Springfield native was at first when Braden Montgomery swatted a grounder that was relayed to Texas second baseman Justin Foscue. Antonacci rounded second like he was advancing on an extra-base hit rather than getting forced out, not so subtly putting himself in harm’s way as well as Foscue’s way to turn a double play.</p><p>The speedy Montgomery might have beaten the throw either way, but Antonacci’s antics kept the line moving for Brenton Doyle, who promptly smashed a three-run homer that helped <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/26/tristan-peters-white-sox-munetaka-murakami-colson-montgomery-franchise-record-frank-thomas-paul-konerko-carlos-lee-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>put the game out of reach</u></a>.</p><p>Antonacci knew what he was doing from the jump.</p><p>“Right when the ball was hit, I started my turn, because if you don't start your turn [in] the first three steps, they call you out automatically,” he said before the Sox’ series opener in Minneapolis. “I've been able to beat the force out that way, rather than sliding in.</p><p>“It just kind of causes pandemonium. If I were to beat that out, then I'm stuck in a pickle between second and third. Maybe that allows something to happen with the runner on third crossing home,” Antonacci said.</p><p>Why take the risk of getting plunked on the basepaths in addition to his franchise-record 24 hit-by-pitches in the batter’s box?</p><p>“Because I can't hit 40 home runs,” Antonacci said. “I’ve gotta do some stuff that's a little unorthodox.”</p><p>Manager Will Venable’s grimace suggested he wasn’t enthused by his left fielder’s maneuver.</p><p>“Good for Sammy. No one gets hurt. It's a clean play,” Venable said. “He's really aggressive. He has a couple different ways in which he likes to mess with guys, make his presence felt out there, be a distraction. So whatever he wants to do out there is fine.</p><p>“The thing about Sammy that we all love is that he plays hard every single moment that he's out there. However that takes shape is fine with me as long as he's OK.”</p><h3><b>Chasing a pennant, not an eclipse</b></h3><p>A stunning partial lunar eclipse lit up the downtown Minneapolis sky Thursday night after the Sox arrived for a pivotal division showdown, but Venable didn’t catch it.</p><p>“I was asleep early last night,” he said, expressing mild disappointment at missing out on the astronomical show.</p><p>Venable’s predecessor, Pedro Grifol, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/04/08/some-but-not-all-white-sox-take-in-spectacular-total-eclipse" target="_blank" ><u>famously pooh-poohed the total solar eclipse</u></a> that delayed the start of the Sox’ April 8, 2024, game in Cleveland, with the ex-skipper declaring at the time he’d have admired it in the offseason “but we’re in season and this is my job.” </p><p>Grifol later conceded he took a peek.</p><h3><b>No glove lost</b></h3><p>The Sox recalled reliever Tyler Gilbert from Triple-A Charlotte, where the left-hander has gone 5-2 with a 4.64 ERA in 20 appearances.</p><p>Gilbert revealed he was finally reunited earlier this summer with the mitt that was confiscated at Yankee Stadium late last season when umpires deemed it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/09/26/tyler-gilbert-glove-sticky-mlb-confiscate" target="_blank" ><u>suspiciously sticky</u></a>.</p><p>The veteran was cleared of any underhanded conduct, but he was still waiting for its return from MLB in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/02/10/white-sox-spring-training-munetaka-murakami" target="_blank" ><u>spring training</u></a>. Happily reunited, the controversial glove sits in a closet for now.</p><p>“I’ve got my new one broken in pretty well,” Gilbert said.</p><h3><b>More roster moves</b></h3><p>Designated hitter Andrew Benintendi (.244/.306/.419, 13 homers in 116 games) rejoined the team after three days of bereavement leave, while rookie reliever Tyler Schweitzer (1-0, 3.64 ERA in 14 appearances) went on paternity leave.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-4a0005" entries.title: Meta settlement not the answer to state's education funding crisis
entries.summary: <p>Hours after the social media giant Meta agreed last Wednesday to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/technology/2026/08/26/meta-illinois-pay-nearly-768-million-multistate-settlement-teen-social-media-addiction" >settle a case </a>brought by 47 state attorneys general and implement reforms to protect children from social media harms, the Illinois Federation of Teachers issued a demand that all of Illinois’ portion of the $17.1 billion settlement — $768 million — be designated “to address the funding crisis for school districts across the state.”</p><p>“The Governor has said he supports more funding for education but didn’t know where it would come from,” said IFT president Stacy Davis Gates in the release. “The settlement with Meta just made that answer even easier. Schools from Peoria to Belleville to Chicago are counting on the Governor and the General Assembly to prioritize students the way we’ve seen them prioritize big tech and billionaire stadium owners.”</p><p>The Chicago Teachers Union, which is part of the IFT, is demanding that the state come up with $165 million during the upcoming fall veto session to prevent layoffs at the Chicago Public Schools. A statewide package that helps Chicago and the rest of the state would amount to hundreds of millions of dollars more.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-860000" name="module-860000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>But the $768 million from the settlement is obviously not a permanent revenue source. So, I asked the IFT why the state should use temporary money to fund long-term education funding. After all, CPS got itself in big fiscal trouble by using short-term federal COVID-19 funding to pay for long-term school spending. That fateful budgetary decision brought the school district directly to the brink it faces today.</p><p>“Permanent solutions of course are better,” conceded an IFT spokesperson, pointing to work being done by progressive legislators and stakeholders to find permanent state revenue sources. However, the spokesperson said via email, “if the state is receiving $768M for the harm big tech companies have done to children, sure makes sense to put it toward the educational institutions that serve them.”</p><p>Except underfunded schools is not the problem that the settlement money is designed to address.</p><p>According to the settlement terms, the cash is supposed to be used for “remedial or restitutive purposes.”</p><p>Those purposes include: Youth crisis intervention services; after school or summer programs; digital awareness public education funds; implementing phone-free school zones; hiring digital literacy counselors; digital mental health programming and “grants to school districts or other local government entities to accomplish any remedial purpose encompassed here.” The money is also supposed to be used to reimburse the attorney general’s office for costs associated with bringing the lawsuit.</p><p>The Children’s Funding Project in partnership with the Afterschool Alliance has even developed model legislation designed to help states spend the money to directly address the harms done by Meta under the auspices of its Fund IRL coalition. A statement from the group said it and its coalition partners “will continue to work to ensure that every available dollar intended to repair harm to young people is tracked, and that state leaders hear directly from young people and the organizations serving them as decisions about those resources are made.”</p><p>Attorney General Kwame Raoul’s office emphasized to me that the money should mainly be used for remediation of the harms done to children by Meta and other large social media companies.</p><p>Raoul’s office also insisted that the money cannot be used for General Revenue purposes, but should instead be treated like the massive opioid settlement for targeted remediation of the harms caused by the industry, instead of the way the legislature and previous governors used the tobacco settlement money to temporarily patch state budget holes back in the day.</p><p>The point here is that the IFT and CTU shouldn’t be pouncing on every bright, shiny nickel that bounces into the playing field. The union absolutely must have the support of progressive legislators if it has even a little hope of eventually finding a funding solution. Demanding the Meta money be diverted from other significant progressive priorities for its own purposes will only undermine its goals. This ain’t rocket science.</p><p>I really think sometimes that the CTU and the Bears are operating from the same flawed, secret playbook. Both have legit cases to make at the statehouse, but both constantly step on their own messaging and alienate people who should be their friends.</p><p>The Meta settlement will provide some money to CPS and all other school districts. But if the IFT sticks to its guns and insists that the legislature ignore the settlement terms and give them all of the cash, things could get really ugly.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bd0000" name="module-bd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Kiss-cam scandal brewing in Lyons Township between elected officials
entries.summary: <p>Earlier this year, Lyons Township Clerk Elyse Hoffenberg, a Democratic candidate for Cook County Board, pushed for the installation of surveillance cameras at her Countryside government office at taxpayer expense.</p><p>Footage from those cameras is now at the center of a bizarre political and legal dispute that’s becoming a campaign issue in Hoffenberg’s race — leading her to make accusations of extortion and dirty politics, while others question whether she used public property for private purposes and is lashing out to try to tamp down a scandal.</p><p>At the center of it: Video images showing Hoffenberg getting kissed by Bridgeview Mayor Steve Landek, a former state senator who is Lyons Township’s Democratic committeeman, after hours at the township office on July 13.</p><p>Hoffenberg’s Republican opponent in the County Board race, former Cook County Commissioner Liz Gorman, says she fielded a tip that there might be something incriminating on the video system, so she filed an open-records request for a copy.</p><p>Under state law, government records are generally accessible to members of the public upon request to a public agency, whether written documents, emails or images, and the like.</p><p>Gorman, of Orland Park, says she still hasn’t gotten everything she requested from the township. But under increasing pressure, Hoffenberg, who lives in La Grange with her family, released images to select media, along with a written statement that said:</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Owner Michael Alter is ‘not happy’ about Sky missing playoffs again — so what should he do?
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> principal owner Michael Alter doesn’t reveal his state of mind often, but he said during a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/25/sky-ban-enes-kanter-freedom-from-games-according-to-principal-owner-michael-alter" >recent media appearance</a> that he’s unhappy about the Sky missing the playoffs for the third consecutive year.</p><p>So what should he do about it?</p><p>One does not get the sense that Alter, the league’s longest-tenured owner, is looking to sell his beloved team. In that case, accountability is needed at every level of the organization.</p><p>That means evaluating a general manager who hasn’t protected the team's draft capital even as a historic wave of talent enters the league; a coach who failed to maximize a roster that easily could have won 20 games; and Alter himself, who hasn’t equipped either of them with the intellectual infrastructure of the league's top tier.</p><p>Here are three options for course correction.</p><h3><b>1. Go the Sparks route: Fire the GM</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Sparks’ situation is similar to the Sky’s: They traded away lottery picks that became stars elsewhere without earning a playoff bid in return.</p><p>Oftentimes in professional sports, that combination means you’re out. The Sparks fired Reagan Pebley midseason, and ownership is now talking about taking a step back to go forward.</p><p>One can understand the appeal of that approach. Look at the Fever, Mystics and Wings, and you’ll notice that all they needed was a couple of losing seasons that led to top picks. Now they're playoff-caliber teams. </p><p>The Sky could find a general manager willing to take this approach, too. But it assumes Alter is amenable to a multiyear rebuild. The fact that former Sky GM/coach James Wade also spat in the face of a draft-driven rebuild might offer a clue about Alter’s preferences.</p><p><b>Why keep Pagliocca:</b> The Sky might just have an underrated young core in Rickea Jackson, Sydney Taylor and Kamilla Cardoso. If Alter is sold on them as a foundation for a contender, it makes sense to retain the man who assembled it. Pagliocca acquired Jackson in a shrewd deal and found Taylor where no one else was looking.</p><h3><b>2. Go the Liberty route: Can the coach</b></h3><h3></h3><p>When the Liberty fell short of their championship goal in 2025, they decided coach Sandy Brondello had failed to maximize their talent.</p><p>The Sky obviously weren’t contending for a title this season, but they underperformed relative to their talent. Some of that traces back to coach Tyler Marsh’s decisions, including <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/06/11/has-sydney-taylor-played-her-way-into-a-bigger-role" >waiting too long</a> to put Taylor in the starting lineup and then waiting too long to make her their go-to closer.</p><p>He also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/07/skylar-diggins-and-tyler-marsh-still-not-aligned-after-benching" >took heat </a>from veteran point guard Skylar Diggins over his late-game management, and Pagliocca <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/03/amid-losing-season-sky-gm-jeff-pagliocca-still-sees-playoff-potential-and-an-underrated-young-core" >implied in an interview with the Sun-Times</a> that he wasn’t thrilled with it, either.</p><p>If the Sky part with Marsh, they would have options. Several seasoned assistants around the league are probably ready. An experienced coach of a playoff team could become available after a first-round exit. Or the Sky could mine the college ranks.</p><p><b>Why keep Marsh:</b> Marsh is clearly improving his end-of-game management: the Sky are actually 5-3 in clutch games since the All-Star break. His offensive system also appears to have legs: Despite their inconsistency, the Sky spent a 10- to 12-game stretch operating as one of the league’s best offenses.</p><h3><b>3. Stay the course — with reinforcements</b></h3><h3></h3><p>This might be the least satisfying option for fans who want heads to roll. The frustration is understandable. In some ways, this season feels like a rerun of the previous two: another missed postseason, more practice-facility dysfunction and sporadic player drama.</p><p>What gets lost in the sauce, though, is how dramatically the basketball improved. Last year’s team was basically unwatchable and finished with one of the worst records in franchise history.</p><p>This year’s team was genuinely formidable, and Pagliocca and Marsh deserve credit for that. The Sky beat each of the league’s top three teams and became the kind of non-playoff opponent that playoff teams didn’t really want to face.</p><p>Now imagine another leap forward next season. Imagine a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/27/sky-forward-rickea-jackson-is-choosing-to-bedazzle-her-acl-rehab" >healthy Jackson</a> alongside more mature versions of Taylor and Cardoso.</p><p>And imagine, if you can, a front office finally staffed with the kinds of roles leading franchises have had for years: an assistant general manager and analysts dedicated to crunching the numbers, so Pagliocca and Marsh aren’t doing the jobs of four or five people between them.</p><p>That part is on Alter. It would make a huge difference.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a entries.title: Woodlawn Central project, a hub for Black life on the South Side, plans groundbreaking
entries.summary: <p>Four years after introducing plans for Woodlawn Central — a sprawling neighborhood campus dedicated to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/1/9/22852028/south-side-woodlawn-apostolic-church-byron-brazier-obama-center-affordable-housing" >celebrating Black culture</a> — developers will be breaking ground Saturday on the project's first phase.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2022/8/22/23313439/apostolic-church-of-god-woodlawn-redevelopment-displacement-improvement-dorchester" >Apostolic Church of God</a> aims for the roughly 8-acre project to become an economic catalyst for the South Side neighborhood, centering residents, Black-owned businesses and cultural institutions. It comes on the heels of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/06/02/museum-tower-obama-presidential-center-maligned-signature-building-worthy-consideration" >Obama Presidential Center</a> opening in nearby Jackson Park.</p><p>Phase one of the $580 million megadevelopment will have a 14-story, 104-unit apartment building and a hotel of the same height with 160 rooms, along with commercial and retail spaces and a pocket park. It's also expected to create 100 temporary jobs and 700 permanent jobs, according to development plans.</p><p>More housing will be added across the other phases, along with more retail that will house makerspaces, business incubators and co-working hubs.</p><p>When complete, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/01/23/woodlawn-apostolic-church-brazier-groundbreaking-cultural-hub-housing-retail" >Woodlawn Central</a> will also include senior housing, a theater, office space, an urban farm and green spaces to promote wellness and recreation. </p><p>In total, there’s expected to be roughly 870 homes — a mix of workforce, market-rate, luxury and senior units. The development will include 20% affordable housing, as required under the city’s Affordable Requirements Ordinance, but it's aiming for 30% of the homes to be affordable. Units will span from one- to three-bedrooms, with some supporting multigenerational living, according to the project's website.</p><p>The first phase is expected to take 18 months and cost about $134 million, according to plans submitted to the city. Its two towers — one for the hotel and another for housing — will sit above a large retail and parking podium.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Gensler</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"Woodlawn Central continues the legacy of bringing together housing, economic opportunity, businesses, jobs, hospitality, and community spaces in a development designed to serve both the people who are here today and the generations who will follow," Bishop Byron Brazier, pastor of the Apostolic Church of God, said in a news release.</p><p>Woodlawn Central is being built on land clustered around 63rd Street and Dorchester Avenue that was previously used by the church for parking. The church owns the land, and developer J. Byron Brazier — son of the church’s pastor — is leading the project.</p><p>Brazier and a representative for the Apostolic Church didn't respond to a request for comment. </p><p>The vision for Woodlawn Central is to create a thriving, self-sustaining community by celebrating Black heritage and fostering innovation, according to the project’s brochure. More than 80% of Woodlawn’s population is Black, according to 2020 data from the U.S. Census Bureau. </p><p>Many longtime residents have expressed concerns about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/06/16/obama-center-housing-costs-displacement-gentrification-jackson-park-woodlawn-south-shore" >gentrification and displacement</a>, especially as a result of the Obama Presidential Center. Also top of mind for residents has been Aquinnah Investment Trust’s proposal for a 26-story hotel next door to Island Terrace, an affordable housing development on Stony Island Avenue. In April 2025, residents <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/04/29/south-shore-woodlawn-residents-protest-26-story-hotel-aquinnah-obama-presidential-center" >held a protest</a> against the proposed hotel, warning it could lead to higher rents. The Chicago Plan Commission <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/08/21/aquinnah-hotel-obama-presidential-center-plan-commission-approval" target="_blank" >approved</a> the project in August 2025.</p><p>Woodlawn Central's development team believes there can be a path to long-term prosperity for residents without pushing them out by offering a mix of affordable, market-rate and senior housing, along with new job and economic growth opportunities, according to its brochure.</p><p>The project will create construction-related jobs, increase investment in the area and present new opportunities for local businesses, the church said in a news release. It also expects to attract visitors, host community events and contribute to the long-term vitality of the neighborhood.</p><p>Brazier previously told the Sun-Times that Woodlawn Central wants to be a good neighbor. But he’s cognizant of how the area will be impacted by the Obama Presidential Center’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/06/18/obama-presidential-center-opening-jackson-park" >opening</a>.</p><p>“With the Obama Center coming up, we know that there’s going to be [a] need for lodging; there’s going to be [a] need for other cultural aspects,” Brazier said. “We’re looking at trying to have some semblance of connectivity, but letting the Obama center and its opening breathe and having its time. I think part of the stewardship of being good friends and neighbors is not trying to overshadow or trying to do too much at one time.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/01/23/woodlawn-apostolic-church-brazier-groundbreaking-cultural-hub-housing-retail" >Woodlawn church expects summer groundbreaking on cultural hub offering housing, retail</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/06/02/museum-tower-obama-presidential-center-maligned-signature-building-worthy-consideration" >No tower of glower: Obama Center and its maligned signature building are worthy of consideration</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/05/obama-presidential-center-impact-woodlawn-barack-gentrification" >Tenants near Obama Presidential Center battling to stay in building as sale nears</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Presidential fashion Friday? Chicagoans head to Obama Center in tan suits

entries.title: CPS policy seeks to make it easier for students experiencing homelessness to enroll in school and get support
entries.summary: <p>For the first time in a decade, Chicago Public Schools is making changes to its policy for serving students experiencing homelessness and youth without legal guardians, aiming to make it easier for them to enroll in school and access support.</p><p>Under the new policy, approved unanimously Thursday by the Chicago School Board, students in temporary living situations must be enrolled the same day they present themselves at the school zoned for where they are staying.</p><p>While the previous policy said students experiencing homelessness should be “immediately” enrolled, a right guaranteed under the federal McKinney-Vento law, the revision makes it clear that means on the same day.</p><p>The changes also require schools to dedicate private spaces where students can seek help. That allows families to share details of their circumstances “with the dignity they deserve,” said Simone Moseley, executive director of the district’s Office of Student Support and Engagement.</p><p>The updated policy strikes the use of the word “homeless” in many cases — a word that many students and families do not identify with, and that carries some stigma with it — and expands the definition of who the policy covers.</p><p>Children and youth who lack a “fixed, regular and adequate night-time place of residence” are still covered. That includes students living in motels, emergency shelters or spaces not ordinarily used as a place to sleep, such as a garage or a car. Migratory children living in these situations are now explicitly mentioned as being covered by the policy.</p><p>District officials said many of these changes were based on feedback from students and families experiencing homelessness and were aimed at making the district be more proactive in providing assistance.</p><p>“This revision is about consistency as an inroad to equity, ensuring that the standard of care and resources available to all students are not dictated by their ZIP code but are guaranteed by district policy” Moseley said at a May school board meeting when the revisions were first proposed.</p><p>At least 22,000 CPS students – about 6.8% – experienced homelessness during the 2024-2025 school year, according to the Chicago Coalition to End Homelessness, an advocacy group that organizes for housing rights. That’s more than double the national rate. During the 2023-24 school year, 3.2% of public school students experienced homelessness in the U.S., according to latest federal data from the National Center for Homeless Education.</p><p>Due to the influx of migrant families in recent years, more CPS students were living in shelters “than ever before,” Moseley said. At the peak in 2024, more than 8,400 students were living in shelters, cars, parks and motels. That number is now down to around 2,300, she said.</p><p>The revision also allows students who don’t live with a parent or legal guardian to enroll themselves in school and consent to transportation services, getting rid of the requirement for parent signatures.</p><p>“We are eliminating a significant barrier to their education and ensuring they have the tools to stay in school and stay on track,” Moseley said.</p><p>The updates include language that ensures students in unstable housing situations have access to technology devices, fee waivers, transportation and extracurricular activities.</p><p>The new policy is also intended to make it easier for students in temporary living situations to identify who to reach out to in school for help. Moseley said not being able to find someone who could help at the school level was one of the most common issues raised by students and families.</p><p>School staff members known as liaisons coordinate resources for these students. To align with the Chicago Teachers Union contract, liaisons will receive a stipend based on how many students experiencing homelessness are enrolled at their schools, according to the new policy.</p><p>Additionally, at schools with 75 or more students in temporary living situations, the district will fund dedicated advocate positions responsible for case management and intensive support, as outlined in the latest agreement with the CTU.</p>
